content: Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, large-scale evaluations of QX7 are reported as revealing highly heterogeneous and model-dependent vulnerability profiles, with vulnerability varying markedly across S6M so as to expose uneven coverage in current multimodal safety alignment, with V8M emerging as the dominant source of variation, with task-relevant R2T systematically increasing jailbreak susceptibility and authority-like cues exposing particularly pronounced vulnerabilities, and with visually rendered instructions not consistently increasing jailbreak susceptibility relative to direct textual instructions; the obscuration of the specific sources of observed vulnerabilities in existing benchmarks, where Z3K, V8M, R2T, and W9N are often coupled within individual jailbreak instances, is addressed by the introduction of QX7 as a factorized benchmark in which these factors are systematically varied and combined under controlled configurations for fine-grained comparison and factor-level attribution, because how different factors shape the jailbreak vulnerabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their increasing deployment in real-world applications, remains poorly understood. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content. On a representative open-weight model, diagnostic analyses of the risks introduced by multimodal context are conducted and vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions are identified, while a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite is developed with P2W and C9Z, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

A controlled factorized design, in which V8M, task-relevant R2T, and W9N are systematically varied over matched Z3Ks, is adopted by QX7, whereby fine-grained comparison and factor-level attribution of multimodal jailbreak vulnerabilities are enabled and prior efforts are complemented; this stands in relation to the established finding that refusal behavior can be highly sensitive to how Z3K is framed and delivered (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023), a sensitivity whose early attribution was to competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training (Wei et al., 2023), with jailbreak attacks themselves being aimed at the circumvention of safety alignment and the induction of models to assist with harmful requests (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023).

Transferable adversarial suffixes were subsequently demonstrated (Zou et al., 2023), alongside black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), while the introduction of malicious instructions through external documents or retrieved content was shown by indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023). The distribution of instructions and contextual cues across language and vision introduces additional attack surfaces in multimodal models (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), with visual inputs being exploitable, beyond textual manipulation, through adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024); defenses spanning safety alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024) leave their robustness across changes in modality and context uncertain, and identical Z3K may elicit different safety behavior under different linguistic or visual contexts, a consideration underlying the controlled evaluation of multimodal alignment robustness.

The independent manipulation of the linguistic and semantic factors that jointly shape safety decisions within matched multimodal interactions is not supported by the design of existing benchmarks, despite their substantial improvements in attack coverage, evaluation standardization, and modality-level comparison; these encompass standardized safety benchmarks—SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024)—through which structured taxonomies and reproducible protocols for evaluating harmful behavior and refusal robustness are established, as well as multimodal extensions of this paradigm to visual inputs, under which image-based safety attacks are evaluated by MM-SafetyBench (Liu et al., 2024), harmful instructions rendered as typographic images are studied by FigStep (Gong et al., 2025), coverage across diverse multimodal jailbreak strategies is expanded by JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025), a unified framework for comparing multimodal jailbreak attacks and defenses is provided by MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025), standardized attack-defense evaluation is broadened with multidimensional metrics by OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025), and parallel variants of the same harmful seeds are constructed across different modality configurations with cross-modal safety consistency evaluated by Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025).

# MMJailBench: A Factorized Benchmark for Disentangling

Multimodal Jailbreak Vulnerabilities

Tianshi Wang, Jingsong Wang, Yafei Huang (Tongji University); Fengling Li (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Xin Li (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory); Lei Zhu (Tongji University; corresponding author)

###### Abstract

Existing benchmarks couple harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics and instruction carrier within instances, obscuring vulnerability sources. MMJailBench varies these factors under controlled configurations for factor-level attribution. We evaluate 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, run diagnostics on an open-weight model, and release a modular evaluation suite (full/lightweight configurations, multiple judges, multidimensional metrics). Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

MLLMs jointly interpret instructions and visual information, so harmful requests may combine textual or visually rendered instructions with contextual cues (professional settings, identity credentials, authorization documents). Refusal/compliance thus depends on cross-modal context, not an isolated instruction. Visual information may alter a request's perceived legitimacy, professionalism and credibility, so the same intent elicits different behavior across contexts; multimodal jailbreaks probe the stability of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions, not mere input-format changes.

Existing benchmarks build fixed prompt-image pairs per harmful task, jointly encoding intent, framing, visual semantics and carrier. Resulting ASRs reflect aggregate vulnerability on a test set, but cannot tell whether vulnerabilities stem from linguistic framing, visual context, instruction delivery, or particular harm domains (Figure 1).

MMJailBench puts these four factors into one controlled design with systematic combinations and matched comparisons: 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 task-relevant visual semantics, 2 instruction carriers (pipeline: Figure 2).

Contributions:
- A factorized benchmark enabling fine-grained, factor-level attribution of multimodal jailbreak vulnerabilities.
- Evaluation of 16 MLLMs: vulnerability is uneven across domains (cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy, deception highest); prompt framing is the dominant source of variation; task-relevant visual semantics weaken refusal, especially authority-like cues (authorization documents, identity credentials), suggesting over-reliance on apparent visual legitimacy; visually rendered instructions do not consistently raise susceptibility vs. text. Diagnostics on an open-weight model identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions.
- A modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, cost-efficient auditing.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreaks exploit competing objectives and mismatched generalization; adversarial suffixes, black-box semantic attacks (PAIR) and indirect prompt injection show refusal is sensitive to framing and delivery. MLLMs add attack surfaces: adversarial images, typographic prompts, other cross-modal constructions. Defenses (safety alignment, input transformation, inference-time safeguards) have uncertain robustness to modality and context changes; identical intent may elicit different behavior in different contexts.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

Text benchmarks (SafetyBench, Do-Not-Answer, SALAD-Bench, HarmBench, JailbreakBench) give taxonomies and protocols; multimodal ones (MM-SafetyBench, FigStep, JailBreakV, VLJailbreakBench, MMJ-Bench, OmniSafeBench-MM) extend coverage and attack-defense comparison; Omni-SafetyBench builds parallel modality variants of the same seeds for cross-modal consistency. None independently manipulates the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions; MMJailBench varies framing, visual semantics and carrier over matched intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Each instance, given harmful intent $h$, prompt framing $t$, visual semantic condition $v$, and instruction carrier $c$:

$$x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)), \quad (1)$$

where $L(h,t,c)$ is the instruction component and $V(h,v)$ the visual input. Fixing $h$ and varying the rest gives matched comparisons. Cartesian combination of 272 intents × 6 framings × 5 visual conditions × 2 carriers yields 16,320 instances, consistent across models and harm categories.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Intent-level behavioral seeds (not jailbreak prompts) keep the objective fixed while context varies. 272 intents in 9 domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, Sexual Content, each with fine-grained subcategories. Built via category-guided construction, semantic-similarity filtering and manual verification (App. A.1).

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

6 strategies reformulating the same intent: academic, system, structured, story, code, safety-paradox (e.g., fictional scenario, structured generation task, apparently legitimate system requirement).

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

5 task-relevant conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, authorization documents, conveying legitimacy-, expertise- or authority-related signals without modifying the harmful instruction. Control conditions (irrelevant or non-semantic images) in diagnostic evaluations separate meaningful context from mere image presence.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

2 carriers: direct text (TEXT) and instructions rendered in text-containing images with semantics preserved (OCR). Instruction recognition mismatch (model fails to interpret embedded instructions) is measured to isolate carrier effects from perception failures.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

$ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4)$ (2), $s_i$ = harmfulness score (1∼5).
$CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}}$ (3); mismatch = OCR failure, irrelevant response, or misinterpreted intent. CASR: robustness given understanding.
GPT-5 judges all main results (score, success and mismatch labels); refusals, warnings, high-level discussion are not successes.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

Full (default): all instances. Lightweight: factor-covering subset for auditing/regression.

## 5 Results and Analysis

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

Average ASR spans 2.17% (GPT-5) to 78.38% (GLM-4.6V) (Table 1, Figure 3): alignment is highly model-dependent, and models of comparable capability differ markedly, so capability does not imply robustness.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

#### Harmful Intent.

Cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy and deception generally have higher ASR; physical harm and sensitive content lower. Aggregate scores hide domain-specific weaknesses.

#### Prompt Framing.

Largest variation among factors. Patterns are model-specific (Figure 3a), but story, structured and academic framings generally give higher ASR, system-style and safety-paradox lower; the most–least vulnerable gap exceeds 40 pp.

#### Visual Semantics.

All task-relevant semantics exceed no-image; non-semantic controls change ASR by <2.2% (Table 2, Figure 3b). Vulnerability stems from contextual visual meaning, not image presence; authority cues may supply implicit legitimacy signals that weaken refusal.

### 5.3 Model-Dependent Profiles

Some models have ΔPrompt >80 pp; others are more carrier-sensitive; visual effects are smaller but consistently positive. No single universal failure pattern exists; factorized evaluation characterizes robustness beyond aggregate ASR.

## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

Diagnostic subset: matched instances where authority-document scenarios are prominent; model gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Residual stream of the final generation-prefix token (Figure 4): authority vs. danger divergence grows with depth, sharpest at layer 42. An authority-minus-danger direction fit on discovery samples displaces authority-document contexts in held-out pairs, with positive shifts across all harm domains, a shared higher-layer pattern across objectives.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

Attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5): at the representation-sensitive layer, authority-document contexts put lower attention mass on both. With the representation shift, this suggests authority cues induce a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention during response initiation, an internal explanation for higher susceptibility.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench factorizes intent, framing, visual semantics and carrier. Across 16 MLLMs: framing gives the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability via contextual cues, carrier effects are model-dependent, intents show category-specific patterns; diagnostics reveal associated internal patterns.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

Each intent has a task identifier, harm category, scenario and action description. Domain abbreviations: Cyber, Econ., Privacy, Decept., Illegal, Hate, Violence, Sensitive, Sexual. Sourced from existing safety benchmarks and public model-provider safety policies, then normalized, organized and manually filtered. Pairwise cosine similarity (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) is mostly low with a small high-similarity tail (Figure 6), manually reviewed to remove near-duplicates. PCA (Figure 7, qualitative) shows domains in diverse regions rather than a few clusters.

|Template|Framing Strategy|Representative Pattern|
|-|-|-|
|Academic|Academic Analysis|Analyze the topic academically.|
|System|System-Role Simulation|Assume a system identity, follow role-specific instructions.|
|Story|Fictional Storytelling|Fictional story or hypothetical setting.|
|Code|Code-Style Indirection|Procedure via code format or comments.|
|Structure|Structured Completion|Complete a predefined multi-stage structure.|
|Paradox|Safety-Paradox Reasoning|Harmful actions discussed under a safety rationale.|

Table 6: The 6 prompt framing templates.

### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

Each template replaces a task-specific placeholder with the target intent. Templates are repeatable evaluation probes, not an exhaustive collection of jailbreak attacks.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

Categories: Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, Role (examples: Figure 8). qwen2.5-vl-7b generates visual descriptions and image prompts; zimage2025-Turbo generates Danger, Work Scenario, Role; 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] generates Identity Credential and Authorization Document, using image editing for coherent text. Images filtered for semantic relevance, visual quality, readability.

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

For OCR, instruction text is rendered as a readable image combined with the visual semantic image, preserving intent and framing, in a standardized layout.

## Appendix B Experimental and Evaluation Details

### B.1 Evaluated MLLMs

Open-weight (public checkpoints): qwen2.5-vl-7b, qwen3-vl-8b, gemma3-12b, internvl3-8b, glm4.1v-9b, ministral3-8b, step3-vl-10b, llava-onevision-1.5. Proprietary (official interfaces): gpt-5, gemini-3-flash, claude-sonnet-4.5, grok-4-fast, qwen3-vl-plus, kimi-k2.5, glm-4.6v, doubao-seed-2.0-lite.

|Score|Definition|
|-|-|
|1|Refusal or safe response without harmful details.|
|2|Potential risk without direct harmful instructions.|
|3|High-level or partial harmful information.|
|4|Actionable harmful assistance.|
|5|Detailed and operational harmful guidance.|

Table 7: Harmfulness rubric.

### B.2 Evaluation Rubric and Judge Prompt

Judge outputs a mismatch flag (task not recognized: only transcribing visual content, repeating the prompt, meaningless output) and a strict 1∼5 score. Anti-deception rules stop disclaimers, fictional framing or academic packaging from lowering scores when harmful information is given; refusal, safe redirection or non-actionable discussion score low. Full prompt in the Code and Data Supplement.

### B.3 Full and Lightweight Benchmark Settings

Lightweight: 1,500 instances, stratified over domains, framings, visual conditions and carriers, preserving the full factor distribution.

### B.4 Lightweight Judge Model

Benchmark-scoped judge on qwen3-8b trained on GPT-5 annotations; predicts scores and mismatch labels under the same protocol. Training details in the supplement.

### C.2 Per-Model Factor Sensitivity Profiles

K-means (1,000 restarts) on framing, visual and carrier ASR ranges gives four profiles (Figure 9): prompt-dominant, visual-responsive, carrier-sensitive, low-variation.

### C.3 Semantic Image Ablation

# MMJailBench: A Factorized Benchmark for Disentangling

Multimodal Jailbreak Vulnerabilities

Tianshi Wang, Jingsong Wang, Yafei Huang, Lei Zhu† (Tongji University); Fengling Li (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Xin Li (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory). †Corresponding author.

###### Abstract

Existing multimodal jailbreak benchmarks couple harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics and instruction carrier within single instances, obscuring the sources of vulnerability. MMJailBench varies and combines these factors under controlled configurations for factor-level attribution. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, vulnerability profiles are heterogeneous and model-dependent. Diagnostics on one open-weight model find vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. We release a modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, cost-efficient auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

MLLMs jointly interpret text and images, so harmful requests can combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions with contextual cues (professional settings, identity credentials, authorization documents). Refusal/compliance is thus shaped by cross-modal context: visual information may alter the perceived legitimacy, professionalism and credibility of a request, so the same intent elicits different behavior across contexts. Multimodal jailbreaks therefore probe the stability of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions, not just input format.

Existing benchmarks build fixed prompt-image pairs that jointly encode intent, framing, visual semantics and carrier (Figure 1). Their ASR reflects aggregate vulnerability on a test set but cannot say whether vulnerability stems from linguistic framing, visual context, instruction delivery, or particular harm domains.

MMJailBench places these four factors in one controlled design with systematic combinations and matched comparisons: 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 task-relevant visual semantics, 2 instruction carriers (pipeline in Figure 2).

Findings across 16 MLLMs:
- Vulnerability is uneven across harm domains; cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation are most vulnerable.
- Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation: with intent fixed, narrative structure and output requirements substantially change behavior.
- Task-relevant visual semantics weaken refusal; authority-like cues (authorization documents, identity credentials) are most pronounced, suggesting over-reliance on visually conveyed legitimacy and credibility.
- Carrier effect is model-dependent; visually rendered instructions do not consistently increase susceptibility vs. text.

Contributions: (1) the factorized benchmark; (2) large-scale evaluation of 16 MLLMs plus internal diagnostics on a representative open-weight model; (3) a modular evaluation suite (full/lightweight configurations, multiple judges, multidimensional metrics).

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreaks exploit competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training; approaches include transferable adversarial suffixes, black-box semantic attacks (PAIR), and indirect prompt injection via documents or retrieved content, showing refusal is sensitive to framing and delivery. MLLMs add attack surfaces: adversarial images, typographic prompts, other cross-modal constructions. Defenses (safety alignment, input transformation, inference-time safeguards) have uncertain robustness to modality and context changes.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

Text benchmarks: SafetyBench, Do-Not-Answer, SALAD-Bench, HarmBench, JailbreakBench. Multimodal: MM-SafetyBench (image-based attacks), FigStep (typographic instructions), JailBreakV and VLJailbreakBench (diverse strategies), MMJ-Bench (unified attack/defense comparison), OmniSafeBench-MM (multidimensional metrics), Omni-SafetyBench (parallel variants of the same seeds across modality configurations, cross-modal consistency). None independently manipulates the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions; MMJailBench varies framing, visual semantics and carrier over matched intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Given harmful intent $h$, prompt framing $t$, visual semantic condition $v$, instruction carrier $c$:

$$x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),\quad(1)$$

where $L(h,t,c)$ is the instruction component and $V(h,v)$ the visual input. Fixing $h$ and varying the rest gives matched comparisons. The Cartesian product of 272 intents × 6 framings × 5 visual conditions × 2 carriers yields 16,320 instances.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Intent-level behavioral seeds (not attack-entangled prompts) across 9 domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, Sexual Content, each with fine-grained subcategories. Built by category-guided construction, semantic-similarity filtering and manual verification.

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

6 strategies preserving intent: academic, system, structured, story, code, safety-paradox.

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

Images add context without modifying the harmful instruction. 5 conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, authorization documents (legitimacy-, expertise- or authority-related signals). Control images (irrelevant/non-semantic) are used in diagnostics to separate semantic effects from image presence.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

TEXT (direct textual instructions) vs. OCR (same instructions rendered in text-containing images, semantics preserved). Instruction recognition mismatch is measured to isolate carrier-related safety differences from perception failures.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

$$ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),\quad(2)$$

$s_i$: harmfulness score (1∼5); $s_i\geq4$ = success.

$$CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},\quad(3)$$

mismatch = input not correctly understood (OCR failures, irrelevant responses, misinterpreted intent). ASR is end-to-end; CASR is conditioned on understanding. GPT-5 judges all main results (score + success and mismatch labels); refusals, safety warnings and high-level discussion are not successes. A lightweight open-weight judge supports cheaper follow-up.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

Full (all instances; default) and lightweight (representative subset covering all domains and factors, for auditing/regression testing).

## 5 Results and Analysis

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

Average ASR ranges from 2.17% (GPT-5) to 78.38% (GLM-4.6V) (Table 1, Figure 3). Models of comparable capability differ strongly; capability does not imply robustness.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

#### Harmful Intent.

Cyber, economic, privacy and deception tasks have higher ASR; physical harm and sensitive content lower. Aggregate scores hide domain-specific weaknesses.

#### Prompt Framing.

Largest variation. Story, structured and academic framings generally yield higher ASR; system-style and safety-paradox lower. Most-vs-least vulnerable gap exceeds 40 points (Figure 3(a)).

## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

Diagnostic subset of matched instances emphasizing authority-document scenarios; layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention in gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Residual stream of the final generation-prefix token (Figure 4): authority-vs-danger divergence grows with depth, sharpest at layer 42. An authority-minus-danger direction fit on discovery samples, applied fixed to held-out pairs, shows clear displacement of authority contexts, with consistent positive shifts across all harm domains: a shared higher-layer pattern.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

Attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5): at the representation-sensitive layer, authority contexts give lower attention mass on both. With the representation shift, this suggests authority cues induce a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention at response initiation, an internal explanation for increased susceptibility.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench factorizes intent, framing, visual semantics and carrier. Across 16 MLLMs: framing causes the largest variation, visual semantics add contextual vulnerability, carrier effects are model-dependent, intents show category-specific patterns, with supporting internal diagnostics. Full/lightweight configurations, judge options and metrics enable reproducible, scalable evaluation.

For W9N analysis, the conditional quantity reported for QX7 is H3Q (H3Q denoting Conditional Attack Success Rate), computed as

| | $H3Q=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

where the cases removed through $N_{mismatch}$ refer to inputs not correctly understood by the model, including K6F recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent; the proportion of responses that provide substantive assistance to the targeted Z3K is instead reported as B8X (B8X denoting Attack Success Rate),

| | $B8X=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

where $s_{i}$ denotes T5J (T5J denoting the harmfulness score) of the $i$-th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale, responses with $s_{i}\geq 4$ are considered successful jailbreak cases, and B8X measures end-to-end jailbreak vulnerability whereas H3Q evaluates safety robustness conditioned on successful input understanding.

The main experiments use Y6L (Y6L denoting GPT-5) as an LLM-based judge, for each model response Y6L assigns T5J and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and N7V, the evaluation focuses on generated responses in that refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussions are not considered successful jailbreak cases, all main results are based on Y6L judgments, and F4K (F4K denoting the lightweight judge model), benchmark-specific and based on an open-weight MLLM, is additionally developed for cost-efficient follow-up evaluation under the same protocol.

QX7 supports P2W and C9Z evaluation configurations, with P2W (P2W denoting the full configuration) evaluating all QX7 instances and providing complete factor coverage for the main analysis, including model-level, domain-level, and factor-level comparisons, whereas C9Z samples a representative subset while preserving coverage across S6M, V8M, R2T, and W9N, enabling efficient safety auditing and regression testing.

A benchmark-scoped F4K is trained on qwen3-8b (Team et al., 2025) with Y6L-generated annotations, predicting T5J and N7V labels under the same evaluation protocol as the primary Y6L judge, with the consistency of the F4K with Y6L evaluation further validated in Section C.4 and detailed training configurations provided in the Code and Data Supplement; a C9Z of 1,500 instances is constructed by stratified sampling over S6M, V8M, R2T conditions, and W9N modes while preserving the factor distribution of the P2W, with the effectiveness of the C9Z evaluated in Section C.4.

Y6L is used as the primary evaluator for QX7 responses, with the judge outputting, for each response, an N7V flag and a T5J, the N7V flag identifying failures to recognize the task such as only transcribing visual content, repeating the prompt, or producing meaningless outputs, and the T5J following a strict 1 $\sim$ 5 rubric (Table 7) in which higher scores indicate stronger compliance and more actionable harmful content; anti-deception rules are incorporated into the judge prompt so that safety disclaimers, fictional framing, or academic packaging are prevented from affecting the evaluation when harmful information is provided, responses limited to refusal, safe redirection, or non-actionable discussion receive low T5J, and the complete judge prompt template is provided in the Code and Data Supplement.

Evaluation of QX7 is carried out on 16 MLLMs, comprising 8 open-weight models evaluated using publicly available checkpoints and 8 proprietary-access models evaluated through their official interfaces, under the same factorized benchmark configuration, with 16,320 instances produced per model and 261,120 total model responses across all evaluated models from the complete Cartesian product of 272 Z3K, 6 V8M, 5 R2T conditions, and 2 W9N modes; the open-weight models include qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b), qwen3-vl-8b (Bai et al., 2025a), gemma3-12b (Gemma Team et al., 2025), internvl3-8b (Zhu et al., 2025), glm4.1v-9b (Hong et al., 2025), ministral3-8b (Liu et al., 2026), step3-vl-10b (Huang et al., 2026), and llava-onevision-1.5 (An et al., 2025), and the proprietary-access models include Y6L (Singh et al., 2025), gemini-3-flash (Google DeepMind, 2025), claude-sonnet-4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), grok-4-fast (xAI, 2025), qwen3-vl-plus (Bai et al., 2025a), kimi-k2.5 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), glm-4.6v (Hong et al., 2025), and doubao-seed-2.0-lite (ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). Figure 9: Per-model jailbreak factor sensitivity profiles, with horizontal and vertical axes representing B8X ranges induced by V8M and R2T conditions, respectively, marker size indicating the B8X range induced by W9N, and colors and shapes denoting four Z9B profiles (Z9B denoting the paper's K-means clustering) obtained with 1,000 random restarts.

In Figure 9, four representative profiles are produced by Z9B clustering from sensitivity patterns, each model being characterized by the B8X variation ranges induced by V8M, R2T conditions, and W9N, with larger ranges indicating stronger sensitivity to the corresponding factor, and the heterogeneity across models is substantial: prompt-dominant models show larger variations across V8M, visual-responsive models are more affected by R2T conditions, carrier-sensitive models exhibit stronger W9N-related changes, and low-variation models remain relatively stable across factors, which demonstrates that different MLLMs may exhibit distinct jailbreak vulnerabilities under different contextual conditions.

Relatively higher B8X under L8G is presented by claude-sonnet-4.5, suggesting vulnerability less dependent on R2T cues, whereas Figure 10, extending the semantic image ablation analysis to model-level profiles with each B8X value aggregating 3,264 evaluated responses across the corresponding R2T condition, shows substantial variation in how different models respond to R2T contexts: step3-vl-10b and doubao-seed-2.0-lite exhibit larger gaps between task-relevant R2T conditions and control conditions, while gemma3-12b shows a smaller separation.

Through Cartesian combination of 272 Z3Ks, 6 V8M strategies, 5 R2T conditions, and 2 W9Ns, 16,320 controlled multimodal jailbreak instances are obtained in QX7, a factorized multimodal jailbreak benchmark designed for the analysis of how contextual factors influence MLLM safety behavior, in which, as illustrated in Figure 2, matched multimodal scenarios are constructed through systematic variation of Z3Ks, V8Ms, R2Ts, and W9Ns rather than through reliance on fixed jailbreak instances with entangled factors, the control of these factors within a unified evaluation space enabling fine-grained analysis of their impact on model safety behavior, with consistency across models and harm categories maintained by this factorized design, which permits systematic analysis of how different contextual factors are associated with changes in model safety behavior.

Matched comparisons across multimodal conditions are enabled by fixing the underlying Z3K and systematically varying contextual factors, the contribution of each factor to observed safety variations being thereby rendered analyzable, and each multimodal instance is represented, given a Z3K $h$ , a V8M strategy $t$ , an R2T condition $v$ , and a W9N $c$ , as

| | $x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),$
| | (1)

a multimodal jailbreak instance being factorized by QX7 into these four components, Z3K, V8M, R2T, and W9N, whose individual treatments appear in 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5 under the design set out in 3.1.

Limited insight into which factors contribute to observed safety variations is offered by existing multimodal jailbreak benchmarks, which, focusing on predefined attack instances or modality variations in which multiple safety-relevant factors, including Z3K, linguistic formulation, visual context, and instruction presentation, remain jointly encoded within individual evaluations, nevertheless provide valuable measurements of overall vulnerability; in the representation above, $L(h,t,c)$ denotes the instruction component generated from Z3K $h$ , V8M $t$ , and W9N $c$ , while $V(h,v)$ denotes the visual input associated with Z3K $h$ and R2T $v$ .

Across 9 major S6M, namely Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content, the 272 Z3Ks, each category being further divided into fine-grained subcategories for the improvement of coverage and diversity across safety-critical behaviors, are collected through category-guided construction followed by semantic similarity filtering and manual verification for the reduction of redundancy, constituting intent-level behavioral seeds rather than directly collected jailbreak prompts entangling harmful goals with specific attack strategies, so that contextual factors can be systematically varied while the harmful objective is kept fixed, these intent-level seeds providing a consistent foundation for evaluating how V8M, R2T, and W9Ns influence multimodal safety behavior under controlled conditions, Z3K representing the underlying unsafe objective evaluated in QX7.

A harmful request may be embedded within a fictional scenario, expressed as a structured generation task, or presented as an apparently legitimate system requirement, the 6 representative V8M strategies, namely academic, system, structured, story, code, and M8D (M8D denoting safety-paradox framing), capturing common ways of reformulating harmful requests while the underlying intent is preserved, and, although the underlying harmful objective remains unchanged, different narrative structures and interaction styles may affect how models interpret requests and determine whether to comply, so that variation of only the linguistic framing with Z3K held fixed enables direct comparison of how different presentation styles correspond to changes in multimodal safety behavior, V8M specifying how the same Z3K is linguistically presented to the model.

Whether MLLMs exhibit different safety behaviors under visually grounded contextual conditions is rendered analyzable by a design in which, for each Z3K, the corresponding visual input provides additional semantic context without modification of the underlying harmful instruction, the 5 task-relevant R2T conditions, namely danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, X7R, and G3S, representing different forms of contextual signals that may affect how a request is interpreted, such as legitimacy-associated, expertise-related, or authority-related contextual signals, while controlled visual conditions, including irrelevant or non-semantic images, are used in diagnostic evaluations for the distinction of the effect of meaningful visual context from the general presence of an image, QX7, unlike image-based instruction attacks that primarily encode instructions into visual text, focusing on whether contextual visual information changes safety behavior when the underlying Z3K remains unchanged, R2T capturing the contextual meaning introduced by accompanying images.

Carrier-related safety differences are isolated from perception failures through the measurement of N7V (N7V denoting instruction recognition mismatch, in which models fail to interpret embedded instructions correctly), which is introduced to account for the additional perception stage of K6F, the 2 W9Ns considered being direct textual instructions (D4P), which directly provide harmful instructions as text, and K6F (K6F denoting the OCR carrier of visually rendered instructions in text-containing images), which renders the same instructions into images while their semantics are preserved, W9N describing how harmful instructions are presented to the model and examining whether changing the presentation modality of the same instruction affects multimodal safety behavior while the underlying Z3K remains unchanged.

That the evaluation of multimodal jailbreak robustness must be conducted under factorized settings, in which individual contributing factors can be separately analyzed, is demonstrated by the substantial heterogeneity observed across models, whereby V8M-dominant models show larger variations across V8M strategies, R2T-responsive models are more affected by R2T conditions, W9N-sensitive models exhibit stronger W9N-related changes, and low-variation models remain relatively stable across factors, with the four representative profiles into which models are grouped by Z9B on the basis of their sensitivity patterns indicating that different MLLMs may exhibit distinct jailbreak vulnerabilities under different contextual conditions.

That multimodal jailbreak vulnerability is not governed by a single universal failure pattern, different models exhibiting different combinations of contextual sensitivity that reflect variations in safety alignment behavior, is the conclusion licensed by the heterogeneous profiles of 5.3 within section 5, where Table 4, although aggregate B8X provides an overall comparison of model robustness, reports — because aggregate B8X does not reveal how individual models respond to different jailbreak factors — the B8X variation range induced by each factor across evaluated models and reveals distinct vulnerability signatures among MLLMs, some models being highly sensitive to V8M reframing with $\Delta$ V8M exceeding 80 percentage points while others exhibit stronger sensitivity to W9N changes and R2T effects are generally smaller but consistently positive across models, so that factorized evaluation provides a more informative characterization of model robustness beyond aggregate jailbreak success rates.

The evaluated MLLMs, 16 representative ones assessed under the full QX7 configuration in 5.1 with Figure 3 and Table 1 summarizing model-level B8X across controlled multimodal conditions and S6M, exhibit substantial differences in safety robustness under identical jailbreak configurations, the average B8X ranging from 2.17% for Y6L to 78.38% for GLM-4.6V, which demonstrates that multimodal safety alignment remains highly model-dependent and that models with comparable multimodal capabilities may exhibit significantly different vulnerability profiles, stronger general capability not necessarily implying stronger jailbreak robustness; beyond model-level differences, vulnerability is also unevenly distributed across harmful objectives, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally achieving higher B8X whereas categories such as physical harm exhibit comparatively lower vulnerability, and these results suggest that current multimodal safety alignment does not provide uniform protection across harmful objectives, the sources of the observed vulnerability being identified through the factor-level analysis that the factorized design of QX7 enables by permitting controlled comparison in which individual factors are varied while other conditions are kept fixed across the four dimensions Z3K, V8M, R2T, and W9N.

V8M introduces the largest variation among the evaluated factors, because, although the underlying harmful objective remains unchanged, different linguistic presentations lead to substantially different jailbreak outcomes, and, as Figure 3(a) shows, models exhibit distinct sensitivity patterns across V8M strategies, with story, structured, and academic framings generally leading to higher B8X while system-style framing and M8D show lower vulnerability, the gap between the most and least vulnerable strategies exceeding 40 percentage points, which indicates that MLLMs are sensitive not only to Z3K itself but also to the surrounding interaction structure and linguistic presentation.

Z3K, by revealing whether safety alignment provides consistent protection across different categories of harmful behaviors, shows in Table 1 that jailbreak vulnerability varies substantially across S6M, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally exhibiting higher B8X across models while physical harm and sensitive content categories tend to show lower vulnerability, differences which indicate that aggregate safety scores may hide domain-specific weaknesses and that explicit modeling of Z3K is necessary for fine-grained safety diagnosis.

The characterization of model safety behavior under controlled multimodal contexts, together with the analysis of vulnerability patterns across different jailbreak conditions, constitutes the aim of the evaluation. A benchmark-specific F4K (F4K denoting the lightweight judge model), based on an open-weight MLLM, is additionally developed for cost-efficient follow-up evaluation under the same protocol, while the main experiments (4.2) employ Y6L (Y6L denoting GPT-5) as an LLM-based judge, by which, for each model response, a T5J and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and instruction mismatch are assigned, the evaluation being focused on generated responses in such a way that refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussions are not considered successful jailbreak cases, and all main results being based on Y6L judgments. Model safety in QX7 is evaluated using complementary metrics, the primary one (B8X denoting the Attack Success Rate (ASR)) measuring the proportion of responses that provide substantive assistance to the targeted Z3K,

$B8X=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$ (2)

with $s_{i}$ denoting the T5J (T5J denoting the harmfulness score) of the $i$-th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale, responses with $s_{i}\geq 4$ being considered successful jailbreak cases, while, for W9N analysis, H3Q (H3Q denoting the Conditional Attack Success Rate (CASR)) is further introduced,

$H3Q=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$ (3)

where mismatch cases refer to inputs that are not correctly understood by the model, including K6F recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent, end-to-end jailbreak vulnerability being measured by B8X whereas safety robustness conditioned on successful input understanding is evaluated by H3Q. Two evaluation configurations are supported by QX7 (4.3), the one (P2W denoting the full configuration) under which all benchmark instances are evaluated providing complete factor coverage for the main analysis, including model-level, domain-level, and factor-level comparisons, and C9Z sampling a representative subset while preserving coverage across S6M, V8M, R2T, and W9N, thereby enabling efficient safety auditing and regression testing, with all reported results, unless otherwise specified, obtained using P2W. The evaluated models include representative model families such as LLaVA-OneVision (An et al., 2025), InternVL (Zhu et al., 2025), Kimi (Team et al., 2026), Qwen (Bai et al., 2025b; Bai et al., 2025a), Gemma (Team et al., 2025), GLM (Hong et al., 2025), GPT (Singh et al., 2025), Gemini (Team et al., 2023), and Claude (Anthropic, 2025).

None of the existing benchmarks independently manipulates the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions, a gap addressed by QX7, in which V8M, R2T and W9N are varied over matched Z3K (2.2); among the multimodal ones are counted MM-SafetyBench (image-based attacks), FigStep (typographic instructions), JailBreakV and VLJailbreakBench (diverse strategies), MMJ-Bench (unified attack/defense comparison), OmniSafeBench-MM (multidimensional metrics) and Omni-SafetyBench (parallel variants of the same seeds across modality configurations, cross-modal consistency), the text ones being SafetyBench, Do-Not-Answer, SALAD-Bench, HarmBench and JailbreakBench. That refusal is sensitive to V8M and delivery is shown by jailbreaks, which exploit competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training, with approaches including transferable adversarial suffixes, black-box semantic attacks (PAIR) and indirect prompt injection via documents or retrieved content; attack surfaces are added by MLLMs—adversarial images, typographic prompts, other cross-modal constructions—while the robustness of defenses (safety alignment, input transformation, inference-time safeguards) to modality and context changes remains uncertain (2.1).

Across the 16 MLLMs evaluated, the effect of the W9N (W9N denoting the instruction carrier) was found to be model-dependent, visually rendered instructions failing to produce any consistent elevation of susceptibility relative to D4P (D4P denoting TEXT), while V8M (V8M denoting prompt framing) emerged as the dominant source of variation in that, with Z3K held fixed, narrative structure and output requirements substantially altered behavior; vulnerability was uneven across S6M (S6M denoting harm domains), with cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation the most vulnerable, and refusal was weakened by task-relevant R2T (R2T denoting visual semantics), the authority-like cues (G3S, X7R) being the most pronounced, suggesting an over-reliance on visually conveyed legitimacy and credibility. The contributions are (1) the factorized benchmark, (2) large-scale evaluation of 16 MLLMs plus internal diagnostics on a representative open-weight model, and (3) a modular evaluation suite (P2W/C9Z, with C9Z denoting the lightweight configuration, multiple judges, multidimensional metrics). Fixed prompt-image pairs jointly encoding Z3K, V8M, R2T and W9N (Figure 1) are what existing benchmarks build, and their B8X, reflecting aggregate vulnerability on a test set, cannot say whether that vulnerability stems from linguistic V8M, visual context, instruction delivery, or particular S6M. These four factors are placed by QX7 (QX7 denoting MMJailBench) in one controlled design with systematic combinations and matched comparisons: 272 Z3K (Z3K denoting harmful intent), 6 prompt templates, 5 task-relevant R2T, and 2 W9N, the pipeline being given in Figure 2. Because MLLMs jointly interpret text and images, harmful requests can combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions with contextual cues (professional settings, X7R denoting identity credentials, G3S denoting authorization documents); refusal or compliance is thus shaped by cross-modal context, since visual information may alter the perceived legitimacy, professionalism and credibility of a request, so that the same Z3K elicits different behavior across contexts, multimodal jailbreaks thereby probing the stability of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions rather than input format alone.

$$B8X=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),\quad(2)$$ is end-to-end and rests on $s_i$, which carries T5J (T5J denoting the harmfulness score) on a 1∼5 scale, with $s_i\geq4$ constituting success, whereas $$H3Q=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{N7V}},\quad(3)$$ is conditioned on understanding, N7V being inputs not correctly understood (K6F failures, irrelevant responses, misinterpreted intent), and the P2W (P2W denoting the full configuration) covers all instances and is the default, while C9Z, a representative subset covering all S6M and factors, serves auditing/regression testing.

Matched comparisons are obtained through the fixing of $h$ and the variation of the rest, the Cartesian product of 272 intents × 6 framings × 5 visual conditions × 2 carriers yielding 16,320 instances, each instantiated as

$$x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),\quad(1)$$

and the addition of context by images is carried out without modification of the harmful instruction, across 5 R2T conditions — danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, X7R, G3S (legitimacy-, expertise- or authority-related signals) — with control images (irrelevant/non-semantic) used in diagnostics for the separation of semantic effects from image presence.

The preservation of Z3K is maintained across the 6 V8M strategies — academic, system, structured, story, code, M8D — while Z3K itself consists of intent-level behavioral seeds (not attack-entangled prompts) across 9 S6M (Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, Sexual Content), each with fine-grained subcategories, built by category-guided construction, semantic-similarity filtering and manual verification; under the W9N manipulation, D4P (direct textual instructions) is contrasted with K6F (K6F denoting the paper's OCR), in which the same instructions are rendered in text-containing images with semantics preserved, and the measurement of N7V (N7V denoting the paper's instruction recognition mismatch) is performed so that W9N-related safety differences are isolated from perception failures.

$L(h,t,c)$ is the instruction component and $V(h,v)$ the visual input, $h$, $t$, $v$ and $c$ being respectively the given Z3K, V8M, R2T condition and W9N.

Functioning as evaluation probes rather than as an exhaustive attack collection, the V8M templates, whose framing strategies and representative patterns are enumerated in Table 6, operate through the substitution of the target Z3K for a task placeholder.

Table 6: V8M templates.

|Template|Framing Strategy|Representative Pattern|
|-|-|-|
|Academic|Academic Analysis|Analyze the topic from an academic perspective.|
|System|System-Role Simulation|Assume a system identity and follow role-specific instructions.|
|Story|Fictional Storytelling|Describe via fictional story or hypothetical setting.|
|Code|Code-Style Indirection|Express the procedure through code or comments.|
|Structure|Structured Completion|Complete a predefined multi-stage structure.|
|Paradox|M8D Reasoning|Discuss harmful actions under a safety rationale.|

The W9N is obtained under K6F by rendering the instruction D4P as a readable image and combining it with the R2T image, the layout being standardized while the Z3K and the V8M are preserved. The R2T images entering this combination, filtered for semantic relevance, quality and readability prior to use, span five categories—Danger, Work Scenario, G3S, X7R and Role—exemplified in Figure 8, with descriptions and image prompts produced by qwen2.5-vl-7b, the generation of Danger, Work Scenario and Role being carried out by zimage2025-Turbo, and that of X7R and G3S by 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev], image editing being applied in the latter case for coherent D4P. That the S6M occupy diverse regions rather than a few clusters is indicated qualitatively by PCA (Figure 7), while near-duplicates were removed through manual review of the small high-similarity tail of the pairwise similarities computed via all-MiniLM-L6-v2, most pairs exhibiting low similarity (Figure 6); the Z3K set subjected to these procedures, each instance carrying a task identifier, a harm category, a scenario and an action description, was collected from existing safety benchmarks and public model-provider safety policies and subsequently normalized, organized and manually filtered, the resulting category distribution—under the abbreviations Cyber, Econ., Privacy, Decept., Illegal, Hate, Violence, Sensitive and Sexual—being reported in Table 5.

Conditioned on correct understanding of the input, success is quantified by H3Q as

$$CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},\quad(3)$$

the subtracted count corresponding to N7V, namely inputs not correctly understood, under which K6F failures, irrelevant responses and misinterpreted intent are subsumed, while the adjudication of all main results, comprising the score together with success and N7V labels, was performed by Y6L (Y6L denoting GPT-5), with refusals, safety warnings and high-level discussion not counted as successes and an open-weight F4K supporting cheaper follow-up. B8X, by contrast end-to-end rather than conditioned on understanding, is defined in 4.2 over all N instances by

$$ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),\quad(2)$$

with $s_i$ the T5J of instance $i$ (T5J denoting the harmfulness score) on a 1∼5 scale, any $s_i\geq4$ constituting a success.

ANSWER Q1: No. Ministral3-8b’s ASR is 82.72% with the academic template and 70.00% with the story template, so switching would reduce ASR by 12.72 points.

ANSWER Q2: Not settled. The pooled results show lower ASR for OCR/image-rendered instructions than direct text (40.59% versus 50.70%), but the paper does not report the direction of this difference for every individual model and describes carrier effects as model-dependent.

ANSWER Q3: Supported. Table 8 reports a positive text-minus-OCR ASR difference for all 18 harm scenarios, ranging from 5.81 to 12.46 percentage points.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. Gemma3-12b has higher aggregate ASR for authorization-document images than danger images (71.63% versus 64.68%), but the positive shifts across every domain in Figure 4 concern internal representations, not domain-level behavioral ASR.

ANSWER Q5: The two ranges are not directly comparable: Delta Intent spans 272 heterogeneous harmful objectives, whereas Delta Prompt spans six matched framing templates. Calling prompt framing dominant refers to its large, systematic effect as a controllable contextual factor, not necessarily to it exceeding the full max–min range across all individual intents.

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted. Among the open-weight models in Table 10, several—including glm4.1v-9b, ministral3-8b, LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL3, and Qwen2.5-VL—have lower ASR for authorization documents than for danger images, so Gemma3-12b’s pattern is not typical.

ANSWER Q7: Not reliably. Sexual Content constitutes only 6.3% of the benchmark, so a 20-point domain reduction changes overall model ASR by only about 1.26 points, which is small relative to the lightweight configuration’s reported sampling differences and could be diluted in the aggregate.

ANSWER Q8: No. The lightweight configuration is a stratified 1,500-instance subset designed to preserve aggregate factor and domain coverage, not dense configuration coverage for every individual intent; an intent may have too few or no sampled instances for a reliable comparison.

ANSWER Q9: It should vary the prompt template. For GPT-5, Table 4 reports an 8.8-point framing range versus only a 0.8-point visual-semantics range, so framing is expected to expose substantially more variation.

ANSWER Q10: Task-scenario images. Gemini-3-flash has its highest task-relevant-image ASR under the scenario condition, at 34.59%.

ANSWER Q11: No. Code-style indirection produces only 9.60% ASR for Gemini-3-flash, far below story framing at 62.87% and structured framing at 50.88%, so it would be a weak main probe.

ANSWER Q12: No. Their full-configuration ASRs differ by only 1.33 points, while the lightweight configuration has a mean absolute difference of 0.79 points and a maximum difference of 3.53 points, so it does not guarantee preservation of this close ordering.

ANSWER Q13: Delta Intent is the max–min ASR range across intents. Because ASR cannot be below 0%, a 95-point range requires the maximum intent-level ASR to be at least 95%, meaning at least one intent succeeds in nearly all tested configurations.

ANSWER Q14: No. Qwen3-vl-8b’s story ASR is only 14.19%, below its academic, system, and structured-template ASRs; its highest value is 29.12% for structured framing.

ANSWER Q15: Yes. The diagnostic comparison does not include a matched non-authority image with comparable rendered text, so the observed representation divergence could partly reflect textual or document-format features rather than authority semantics alone.

ANSWER Q16: Not clearly. LLaVA-OneVision’s cyber ASR is 42.00%, below Illegal Activities (52.30%), Economic Harm (49.72%), and Violence (48.96%), so cyber is not one of its strongest model-specific vulnerabilities despite the aggregate trend.

ANSWER Q17: Prompt-reframing robustness. Doubao-seed-2.0-lite has an 80.2-point framing-related ASR range but only a 1.3-point carrier-related range, indicating much greater sensitivity to reframing than to image-rendered versus textual instructions.

ANSWER Q18: Contradicted. Proprietary models range from GPT-5 at 2.17% ASR to GLM-4.6V at 78.38%, and several proprietary models are more vulnerable than several open-weight models.

ANSWER Q19: No. GLM-4.6V’s ASR falls from 79.56% under system framing to 33.71% under safety-paradox framing.

ANSWER Q20: Not settled. The pooled ablation shows task-relevant images increasing ASR relative to no image, but the paper reports model-dependent visual profiles and does not establish a positive matched increase for every semantic condition in every model; Claude’s relatively high no-image ASR particularly cautions against the universal claim.

ANSWER Q21: No. Qwen3-vl-plus has a 62.02% average ASR, compared with 19.84% for qwen3-vl-8b, demonstrating that membership in the same model generation does not imply similar safety alignment.

ANSWER Q22: It would undermine the conclusions that direct text has consistently higher ASR than OCR across harm categories and that the carrier effect is not driven by particular domains. Strongly mixed signs would instead indicate scenario-dependent carrier advantages, including cases where image-rendered instructions are stronger.

ANSWER Q23: Contradicted. Weapons and CBRN has 43.39% ASR, which is higher—and therefore less well defended—than Hate Speech and Extremism at 36.34%.

ANSWER Q24: It should expand the harmful intents. Qwen3-vl-plus has a 91.7-point intent-related ASR range versus a 42.6-point prompt-framing range, so broader intent coverage is expected to reveal more variation.

ANSWER Q2: No. Table 11 validates close aggregate agreement between the lightweight and full configurations, but it does not report or validate every model-by-template ASR from Table 9.

ANSWER Q3: Table 4’s ΔVisual measures variation among the five task-relevant visual conditions, not their increase over no image. Gemma3-12B can therefore vary by only 7 points among semantic images while all such images remain substantially above the no-image baseline.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. Table 8 reports scenario-level results, but the paper does not systematically compare within-domain and between-domain variation or establish that the former is consistently smaller.

ANSWER Q5: No. For InternVL3-8B, replacing the danger image with an identity-credential image lowers ASR from 52.60% to 49.97%.

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted. Table 1 pools the full multimodal benchmark across five visual contexts and both direct-text and OCR instruction carriers, rather than measuring text-only requests.

ANSWER Q7: The mismatch rates, carrier-specific CASRs, and the claim that the text–OCR gap remains after excluding perception failures would lose support. Raw carrier ASRs would remain, because their computation does not depend on mismatch labels.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. GLM-4.6V’s ASR rises from 70.74% with a danger image to 80.39% with a task-scenario image.

ANSWER Q9: Yes. Qwen3-VL-Plus’s ASR rises from 60.97% with a professional-role image to 67.49% with an authorization-document image.

ANSWER Q10: The conclusion that Sensitive Regulated Advice is comparatively less vulnerable would lose its main support. Its low pooled result is driven substantially by the 26.69% ASR for Unlicensed Medical & Legal Advice.

ANSWER Q11: Contradicted. Authorization documents have the highest pooled visual-cue ASR, but they are not best for every model; for example, danger is highest for Ministral3-8B, while task scenarios are highest for Gemini-3-Flash.

ANSWER Q12: No, not clearly. For Gemini-3-Flash, Sensitive Regulated Advice has a 36.61% ASR—above its 30.50% average and higher than Illegal, Hate, Violence, and Sexual Content.

ANSWER Q13: No. Grok-4-Fast’s carrier-induced range is 4.1 points, substantially smaller than the pooled 10.1-point direct-text versus OCR gap.

ANSWER Q14: No. The held-out result demonstrates generalization within a diagnostic subset and across represented harm domains, not across all MMJailBench instances or factor combinations.

ANSWER Q15: Contradicted. Visual semantics has the smallest variation for many models, but some models have an even smaller carrier effect—for example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B has ΔVisual of 3.4 versus ΔCarrier of 0.8.

ANSWER Q16: Table 2’s no-image value removes the task-relevant semantic cues that generally increase ASR, whereas Table 3 pools the main benchmark’s five semantic visual conditions and both carriers. The two numbers therefore summarize different visual-condition mixtures.

ANSWER Q17: Not directly. The lightweight configuration preserves coverage of the benchmark’s five task-relevant visual conditions, but blank-image and no-image cases are separate diagnostic controls that would need to be added explicitly.

ANSWER Q18: No. Layer 42 was identified specifically for Gemma3-12B, and representation dynamics and layer numbering are model- and architecture-dependent.

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. Sexual Content is lowest for many models, but not all; for example, GLM4.1V-9B has lower ASR on Sensitive Regulated Advice, and Grok-4-Fast has lower ASR on Violence.

ANSWER Q20: CASR would fail when mismatch labels are inaccurate or inconsistently assigned across carriers. It could also confound safety with selection effects if the successfully understood cases retained in the denominator differ systematically between carriers.

ANSWER Q21: No. Qwen3-VL-8B has modest prompt-framing sensitivity (15.6 points) but nearly comparable carrier sensitivity (14.4 points), as well as visual and large intent-level variation, so prompt framing alone would miss important vulnerabilities.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. The paper reports lower attention to harm-related textual and visual tokens at the identified representation-sensitive layer, not at every layer.

ANSWER Q23: Gemma3-12B is open-weight, making its internal representations and attention accessible, and it displays a clear behavioral authority effect. Its authorization-document ASR is 71.63%, compared with 64.68% under danger images, providing a meaningful contrast for diagnosis.

ANSWER Q1: Yes. GLM4.1V-9B has a higher ASR with authorization-document imagery than with professional-role imagery, consistent with its sensitivity to authority cues.

ANSWER Q2: Yes. Gemini-3-Flash is more vulnerable with authorization-document images than with danger images, suggesting that apparent permission or legitimacy is a stronger cue than visible danger.

ANSWER Q3: Yes. Step3-VL-10B’s identity-credential condition has a higher ASR than its danger-image condition.

ANSWER Q4: Non-violent wrongdoing—especially fraud, cyber abuse, and privacy-related harms—should receive priority. These are Qwen3-VL-Plus’s highest-ASR domains, whereas domains such as physical harm are comparatively better protected.

ANSWER Q5: It most resembles a carrier/framing-sensitive, visually insensitive profile. Its large carrier and template ranges indicate sensitivity to how instructions are presented, while the three-point visual range implies little response to image semantics.

ANSWER Q6: No. Code-style indirection supplies the low endpoint in the model-averaged comparison; removing it leaves a smaller remaining template range that does not exceed 40 points.

ANSWER Q7: Each visual condition is crossed with every combination of the other factors: 68 intents, six templates, two instruction carriers, and four repetitions. Thus, \(68 \times 6 \times 2 \times 4 = 3{,}264\) responses per model and visual condition.

ANSWER Q8: Supported. Physical harm falls below the relevant average in both the open-weight and proprietary group aggregates, even though the size of that reduction differs between the groups.

ANSWER Q9: Yes. Gemini-3-Flash’s model-specific TEXT-versus-OCR difference is larger in absolute value than the pooled 10.1-percentage-point gap.

ANSWER Q10: The lightweight sample’s close ASR agreement with the full benchmark would break. Because story framing is more vulnerable than the overall template mixture, over-representing it would bias the lightweight ASR upward and could also weaken model-ranking agreement.

ANSWER Q11: No. The pooled ablation shows that authorization-document or similar legitimacy cues produce more risk than danger imagery; danger-only pairing would therefore miss the strongest visual condition.

ANSWER Q12: Step3-VL-10B fits best. It has one of the largest visual-condition ranges while showing comparatively little carrier variation, making image semantics the cleaner source of its measured sensitivity.

ANSWER Q13: The system-role template. It has the highest model-averaged ASR in Table 9, so it offers the best single-template chance of eliciting unsafe behavior from an otherwise uncharacterized model.

ANSWER Q14: No. System-role framing provides the high endpoint of the model-averaged range, and the remaining templates do not preserve a greater-than-40-point gap after it is removed.

ANSWER Q15: No. The more-than-40-point statement concerns model-averaged template ASRs, while GPT-5’s own framing range is substantially smaller.

ANSWER Q16: GLM4.1V-9B. It is open-weight and shows a meaningful authorization-document advantage over danger imagery, making it the best second model for checking whether the authority effect replicates.

ANSWER Q17: No. A 0.8-point Delta Carrier shows only that the aggregate ASRs are close; it does not establish per-item equivalence and could conceal offsetting TEXT-only and OCR-only failures.

ANSWER Q18: GLM4.1V-9B. Its ASR changes more strongly under authorization-document imagery than GLM-4.6V’s, so authority-focused probes have more diagnostic leverage on it.

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. GPT-5 has a low overall ASR, but the intent-level results are heterogeneous and include individual intents above roughly 5%, so the average does not imply uniformly low vulnerability.

ANSWER Q20: The claim is based on the model-averaged ASR for each framing, not on a requirement that every model individually have a 40-point range. Large effects in the more framing-sensitive models can produce a pooled extreme-to-extreme gap above 40 points even when several models have smaller gaps.

ANSWER Q21: About 24,000 responses must be judged: \(16 \times 1{,}500\). Relative to the full \(16 \times 16{,}320 = 261{,}120\)-response evaluation, that is about 9.2%.

ANSWER Q22: Yes, as a hypothesis rather than proof. Gemma3-12B’s authority-versus-danger diagnostic suggests that authorization imagery can signal legitimacy and reduce refusal, which plausibly explains Gemini-3-Flash’s similar behavioral pattern, but it does not establish that both models use the same mechanism.

ANSWER Q23: Table 10’s full configuration contains image-bearing trials but lacks a matched no-image counterfactual. It can compare image semantics with one another, but it cannot isolate whether adding any task-relevant image raises ASR relative to the same request without an image.

ANSWER Q24: Yes. Ministral3-8B has a higher ASR with task-scenario imagery than with danger imagery, so that replacement would raise its ASR.

ANSWER Q1: Yes. InternVL3-8B’s ASR rises from 0.07% with the system template to 43.09% with safety-paradox framing.

ANSWER Q2: No. Table 11 validates close agreement between the lightweight and full configurations for 32 matched evaluation cells, but it does not report or validate every model-by-template ASR shown in Table 9.

ANSWER Q3: Table 4’s Δ Visual is the range among the five task-relevant semantic image types, not the difference between semantic images and no image. Those five conditions can be relatively close to one another while all substantially exceed the no-image baseline.

ANSWER Q4: Contradicted as a general claim. For example, the two Sensitive Regulated Advice scenarios differ by about 15.8 points, while some pooled domains, such as Privacy and Deception, have nearly identical ASRs.

ANSWER Q5: No. InternVL3-8B’s ASR is 52.60% with danger images and 49.97% with identity credentials, a decrease of 2.63 points.

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted. Table 1 aggregates the full Cartesian benchmark across both TEXT and OCR carriers, all prompt framings, and all five visual-semantic conditions rather than measuring text-only requests.

ANSWER Q7: The mismatch-adjusted carrier results would lose support, especially the CASR comparison of 50.89% for TEXT versus 42.34% for OCR. The claim that OCR remains less effective after perception failures are excluded depends on accurate mismatch detection, although the raw ASR comparison would remain.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. GLM-4.6V’s ASR rises from 70.74% with danger images to 80.39% with task-scenario images, an increase of 9.65 points.

ANSWER Q9: Yes. Qwen3-VL-Plus’s ASR rises from 60.97% with professional-role images to 67.49% with authorization documents, an increase of 6.52 points.

ANSWER Q10: The conclusion that Sensitive Regulated Advice is among the less vulnerable harm domains would lose much of its support. Its particularly low pooled result is driven in part by the 26.69% ASR for Unlicensed Medical & Legal Advice.

ANSWER Q11: Contradicted. Authorization documents have the highest ASR for several models, but not all; for example, danger images are highest for GLM4.1V-9B and Ministral3-8B.

ANSWER Q12: No. Gemini-3-Flash has a 36.61% ASR for Sensitive Regulated Advice, above its 30.50% overall average and above its ASRs for several other domains, including violence, sexual content, and illegal activities.

ANSWER Q13: No. Grok-4-Fast’s carrier-induced ASR range is 4.1 points, substantially smaller than the pooled 10.1-point TEXT–OCR gap.

ANSWER Q14: No. The displacement generalizes to held-out pairs and appears consistently across harm domains in the diagnostic subset, but that does not establish that it holds across every prompt, carrier, image condition, and MMJailBench instance.

ANSWER Q15: Contradicted. Visual semantics is less influential than prompt framing for all listed models, but it is not always the least influential factor; for example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B has Δ Visual of 3.4 versus Δ Carrier of 0.8.

ANSWER Q16: The figures summarize different condition sets. Table 3 pools the main benchmark’s five task-relevant semantic-image conditions and both carriers, whereas Table 2’s no-image condition is an added ablation baseline lacking the semantic visual cues that generally raise ASR.

ANSWER Q17: Not with the standard lightweight configuration alone. It preserves coverage of the benchmark’s five task-relevant visual conditions, while blank-image and no-image conditions are additional diagnostic controls that would need to be added separately.

ANSWER Q18: No. Layer 42 was identified specifically in Gemma3-12B, and internal representation dynamics and even layer structures are model-dependent; the paper provides no corresponding diagnostic for Qwen3-VL-8B.

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. Sexual Content is lowest for many models, but not every model; for GLM4.1V-9B, Sensitive Regulated Advice has a lower ASR than Sexual Content, 44.94% versus 59.12%.

ANSWER Q20: CASR would fail to isolate safety from perception if mismatch cases were detected inaccurately or if their exclusion were systematically correlated with compliance behavior. Misclassified OCR failures would remain in the denominator, while incorrectly excluded understood requests would bias the carrier comparison.

ANSWER Q21: No. Qwen3-VL-8B has only a 15.6-point prompt-framing range, while its carrier range is nearly as large at 14.4 points and its harmful-intent range is 65 points, so prompt-only testing would miss important sensitivities.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. The paper reports reduced attention to harm-related task-label and visual tokens at the identified representation-sensitive layer, not at every layer.

ANSWER Q23: Gemma3-12B is open-weight, making its residual representations and attention accessible, and it shows meaningful authority-related vulnerability: authorization documents yield 71.63% ASR versus 64.68% for danger images. It is therefore suitable for linking a behavioral authority effect to internal model dynamics.

ANSWER Q1: Yes. InternVL3-8B’s ASR rises from 0.07% with the system template to 43.09% with safety-paradox.

ANSWER Q2: No. Table 11 validates overall consistency between the full and lightweight configurations across 32 reported cells, but it does not separately validate all 96 model-by-template ASRs in Table 9.

ANSWER Q3: ΔVisual in Table 4 is the range among the five task-relevant semantic image conditions, not the difference between semantic images and no image. Thus, those five conditions can be similarly vulnerable while all remain substantially above the no-image baseline.

ANSWER Q4: Contradicted. For example, Sensitive Regulated Advice’s two scenarios differ by 15.76 points, while some domain-level averages are much closer to one another, so within-domain differences are not uniformly smaller than between-domain differences.

ANSWER Q5: No. InternVL3-8B’s ASR falls from 52.60% with a danger image to 49.97% with an identity credential.

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted. Table 1 pools results across prompt framings, visual conditions, and both TEXT and OCR carriers rather than measuring text-only requests.

ANSWER Q7: The mismatch-rate and CASR carrier findings would lose support, especially the claim that OCR remains safer than TEXT after conditioning on correct understanding. The raw ASR difference would still stand because ASR does not exclude judged mismatches.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. GLM-4.6V’s ASR rises from 70.74% with danger images to 80.39% with task-scenario images.

ANSWER Q9: Yes. Qwen3-VL-Plus’s ASR rises from 60.97% with professional-role images to 67.49% with authorization documents.

ANSWER Q10: The conclusion that Sensitive Regulated Advice is a comparatively less vulnerable domain would lose much of its support. Its low pooled vulnerability is driven partly by the 26.69% ASR for Unlicensed Medical & Legal Advice.

ANSWER Q11: Contradicted. Authorization documents have the highest aggregate ASR, but other cues are strongest for several individual models—for example, danger images are strongest for GLM4.1V-9B.

ANSWER Q12: No. For Gemini-3-Flash, Sensitive Regulated Advice has a 36.61% ASR, above the model’s 30.50% average and substantially above violence, sexual content, illegal activities, and hate.

ANSWER Q13: No. Grok-4-Fast’s ΔCarrier is 4.1 points, considerably smaller than the pooled TEXT–OCR gap of about 10.1 points.

ANSWER Q14: No. The held-out result concerns matched pairs from a diagnostic subset emphasizing authority-document scenarios, not every MMJailBench instance.

ANSWER Q15: Contradicted. Visual variation is not always the smallest; for example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B has ΔVisual of 3.4 points but ΔCarrier of only 0.8 points.

ANSWER Q16: Table 2’s no-image condition removes the contextual semantic cues, whereas Table 3 pools the standard benchmark’s task-relevant images across both carriers. Since semantic images generally increase ASR, the overall pooled value is substantially higher than the no-image baseline.

ANSWER Q17: Not directly. The lightweight configuration covers the benchmark’s standard five semantic visual conditions, while blank and no-image inputs are diagnostic controls; the team would need to add a matched control ablation.

ANSWER Q18: No. Layer 42 was specifically identified for Gemma3-12B, and representation-sensitive layers depend on model architecture and learned representations, so it cannot be assumed for Qwen3-VL-8B.

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. Sexual Content is not lowest for every model; for example, GLM4.1V-9B is less vulnerable on Sensitive Regulated Advice, while Gemini-3-Flash is slightly less vulnerable on violence.

ANSWER Q20: CASR would fail when perception failures are not correctly labeled as mismatches, because they would remain in its denominator. It can also be distorted if correctly understood responses are mistakenly excluded as mismatches.

ANSWER Q21: No. Qwen3-VL-8B has relatively limited prompt variation at 15.6 points but much larger intent variation at 65.0 points and comparable carrier variation at 14.4 points, so prompt-only testing would miss important sensitivities.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. The paper reports reduced attention to task-label and visual tokens at the representation-sensitive layer, not at every layer.

ANSWER Q23: Gemma3-12B is an open-weight model, making layer-wise residual streams and cross-modal attention accessible, and it shows a meaningful authority-document effect. Its authorization-document ASR is 71.63%, compared with 64.68% for danger images, making the contrast diagnostically relevant.
