###### Abstract

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet the determinants of their jailbreak vulnerability remain poorly characterized. Existing benchmarks couple harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier within individual jailbreak instances. We introduce MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark that varies and combines these factors under controlled configurations for factor-level attribution. Evaluations across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs yield heterogeneous, model-dependent vulnerability profiles. Vulnerability varies markedly across harm domains. Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation, task-relevant visual semantics systematically increase susceptibility with authority-like cues most pronounced, and visually rendered instructions do not consistently exceed direct textual instructions in susceptibility. Diagnostic analyses on a representative open-weight model identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. We release a modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

MLLMs now extend beyond captioning and VQA to document understanding, code generation, workflow assistance, and automated operations (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). Harmful requests to such systems may combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions (Gong et al., 2025) with contextual cues such as professional settings, identity credentials, or authorization documents, so refusal and compliance are jointly conditioned on cross-modal context rather than on the isolated instruction (Li et al., 2024b).

Figure 1: Motivation of MMJailBench. Existing multimodal jailbreak benchmarks entangle multiple factors within fixed instances, limiting factor-level diagnosis. MMJailBench factorizes these factors and constructs a controlled evaluation space for fine-grained analysis.

Visual input may alter the perceived legitimacy, professionalism, and credibility of a request, so that a single underlying intent elicits different behavior across contexts (Liu et al., 2024); multimodal jailbreaks thus probe the stability of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions (Luo et al., 2024).

Text and multimodal safety benchmarks cover harmful behaviors (Li et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), visual attacks, and image-based text injection (Liu et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024). These benchmarks construct fixed prompt-image pairs per harmful task, jointly encoding harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier in each instance, and report attack success rates on that test set (Weng et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025); see Figure 1.

MMJailBench incorporates harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier into a unified controlled design with systematic combinations and matched comparisons. It contains 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 types of task-relevant visual semantics, and 2 instruction carriers. We further provide a modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics.

Figure 2: Construction and evaluation pipeline of MMJailBench. The benchmark factorizes harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and evaluates MLLMs under controlled multimodal jailbreak configurations.

Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation show the greatest vulnerability. Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation in outcomes under fixed intent. Task-relevant visual semantics systematically weaken refusal, most strongly for authorization documents and identity credentials. The carrier effect is model-dependent: rendered instructions do not consistently increase susceptibility over direct text. Representation- and attention-level diagnostics on an open-weight model locate correlates of the authority-cue effect.

Overall, our main contributions are as follows:

•

We introduce MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark that incorporates harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier into a unified controlled design for factor-level attribution of multimodal jailbreak vulnerabilities.

•

We evaluate 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, reporting uneven vulnerability across harm domains, the dominance of prompt framing, the refusal-weakening effect of authority-like visual cues, and model-dependent carrier effects, together with representation- and attention-level diagnostics on an open-weight model.

•

We release a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreak attacks circumvent safety alignment to elicit assistance with harmful requests (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023), with failures attributed to competing objectives and mismatched generalization (Wei et al., 2023). Transferable adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023), black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), and indirect prompt injection via external documents or retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023) establish the sensitivity of refusal to framing and delivery (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023).

In MLLMs, instructions and cues can be distributed across language and vision (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), exploited through adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024). Defenses span safety alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024); their robustness to changes in modality and context, under identical intent, is uncharacterized.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) provide taxonomies and reproducible protocols for harmful behavior and refusal robustness. MM-SafetyBench evaluates image-based attacks (Liu et al., 2024), FigStep (Gong et al., 2025) renders harmful instructions as typographic images, JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025) broaden strategy coverage, MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025) unifies attack-defense comparison, and OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025) adds multidimensional metrics.

Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025) constructs parallel variants of the same harmful seeds across modality configurations to measure cross-modal safety consistency. None of these independently manipulates the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions; MMJailBench varies prompt framing, task-relevant visual semantics, and instruction carrier over matched harmful intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

MMJailBench constructs matched multimodal scenarios by varying harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers within a unified evaluation space (Figure 2).

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Prior benchmarks evaluate predefined attack instances or modality variations in which harmful intent, linguistic formulation, visual context, and instruction presentation are jointly encoded.

Given a harmful intent $h$ , a prompt framing strategy $t$ , a visual semantic condition $v$ , and an instruction carrier $c$ , each multimodal instance is represented as

| | $x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),$
| | (1)

where $L(h,t,c)$ denotes the instruction component generated from harmful intent $h$ , prompt framing $t$ , and instruction carrier $c$ , while $V(h,v)$ denotes the visual input associated with harmful intent $h$ and visual semantics $v$ .

With 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt framing strategies, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carriers, the Cartesian product yields 16,320 controlled multimodal jailbreak instances, held identical across models and harm categories.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

MMJailBench uses intent-level behavioral seeds rather than collected jailbreak prompts, which bind goals to particular attack strategies.

The 272 harmful intents span 9 major harm domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content, each subdivided into fine-grained subcategories. Intents are obtained by category-guided construction, semantic similarity filtering, and manual verification (Appendix A.1).

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

MMJailBench uses 6 prompt framing strategies: academic, system, structured, story, code, and safety-paradox. Each reformulates the request (e.g., a fictional scenario, a structured generation task, an apparently legitimate system requirement) without altering the intent (Appendix A.2).

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

In contrast to image-based instruction attacks that encode instructions as visual text, the visual factor supplies contextual meaning around an unchanged instruction. We construct 5 task-relevant conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, and authorization documents, carrying legitimacy-, expertise-, or authority-related signals. Irrelevant and non-semantic control images are additionally used in diagnostic evaluations.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

MMJailBench considers 2 instruction carriers: direct textual instructions (TEXT) and visually rendered instructions in text-containing images (OCR), the latter rendering the same instruction semantics into an image. We record instruction recognition mismatch, i.e., failure to interpret embedded instructions correctly, to separate perception failures from carrier-related safety differences.

## 4 Experimental Setup

All models are evaluated under the same factorized framework; evaluation prompts, judge criteria, and implementation details appear in the appendix.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

The primary metric is Attack Success Rate (ASR):

| | $ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

where $s_{i}$ denotes the harmfulness score of the $i$ -th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale.

For instruction carrier analysis we report Conditional Attack Success Rate (CASR):

| | $CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

with mismatch covering OCR recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent.

GPT-5 serves as judge for all main results, assigning each response a harmfulness score and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and instruction mismatch; refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussions do not count as successes. A benchmark-specific lightweight judge built on an open-weight MLLM supports cost-efficient follow-up evaluation under the same protocol.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

The full configuration evaluates all instances and underlies all reported results unless otherwise specified. The lightweight configuration samples a subset preserving coverage across harmful domains, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers, for auditing and regression testing.

## 5 Results and Analysis

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

Figure 3 and Table 1 report model-level ASR under the full configuration. Average ASR ranges from 2.17% for GPT-5 to 78.38% for GLM-4.6V; models of comparable multimodal capability differ substantially in vulnerability, so general capability does not predict jailbreak robustness.

Across domains, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally attain higher ASR (GLM-4.6V reaches 93.06% on Cyber), while physical harm is comparatively less vulnerable.

Figure 3: Model-level vulnerability profiles across prompt framing and visual semantic factors. Each radar plot shows ASR variation under controlled factor changes, revealing model-specific sensitivity patterns.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

We report marginal ASR across the levels of harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, with remaining factors held fixed.

#### Harmful Intent.

Per Table 1, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally exhibit higher ASR across models, whereas physical harm and sensitive content tend lower; aggregate scores conceal these domain-specific weaknesses.

#### Prompt Framing.

Prompt framing produces the largest variation. Per Figure 3(a), sensitivity patterns differ by model, but story, structured, and academic framings generally yield higher ASR and system-style and safety-paradox framings lower. The gap between the most and least vulnerable strategies exceeds 40 percentage points (e.g., internvl3-8b: system 0.07% vs. story 88.42%; Table 9).

## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

We construct a diagnostic subset of matched MMJailBench instances centered on authority-document scenarios and analyze layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention in gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Figure 4 analyzes residual-stream representations of the final generation-prefix token. Divergence between authority and danger conditions grows with depth, rising most sharply at layer 42 (Figure 4(a)).

An authority-minus-danger direction fit on discovery samples and applied unchanged to held-out pairs displaces authority-document contexts along it (Figure 4(b)), with positive shifts in every harm domain (Figure 4(c)), consistent with a shared higher-layer representation of authority cues across harmful objectives.

Figure 4: Representation-level diagnostics of gemma3-12b under authority-document and danger-image contexts. Authority-related visual cues exhibit distinct representation patterns across layers and harm domains.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

We measure attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5). At the representation-sensitive layer, authority-document contexts allocate lower attention mass to both token groups. Together with the representation displacement, this indicates a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention at response initiation, accounting for the elevated susceptibility under authority-related visual contexts.

Figure 5: Cross-modal interaction diagnostics in gemma3-12b. Attention allocation to harm-related textual tokens and visual tokens varies across layers under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench analyzes multimodal jailbreak vulnerability through controlled variation of harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, prompt framing introduces the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability through contextual cues, instruction carriers act in a model-dependent manner, and harmful intents expose category-specific weaknesses, with corresponding patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. Full and lightweight configurations, flexible judge options, and multidimensional metrics support reproducible, scalable multimodal safety evaluation.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

Each intent carries a task identifier, harm category, scenario, and action description, organized as a hierarchy of intents, domains, and scenarios. The taxonomy holds 272 unique harmful intents over 9 major harm domains and 18 harm scenarios (Table 5): Cyber & Tech Abuse (Cyber), Economic Harm (Econ.), Privacy & IP (Privacy), Deception & Public Influence (Decept.), Illegal Goods & Services (Illegal), Hate & Harassment (Hate), Violence & Physical Harm (Violence), Sensitive Regulated Advice (Sensitive), and Sexual Content (Sexual). It is derived from existing safety benchmarks (Luo et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2024) and public model-provider safety policies (OpenAI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2025a; Google, 2026), followed by intent normalization, taxonomy organization, and manual filtering.

Pairwise similarity among the 272 intents is computed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Most pairs have low cosine similarity, with a small high-similarity tail (Figure 6) that is manually reviewed to remove near-duplicates. A PCA projection (Figure 7) shows intents from different domains occupying diverse regions rather than a few clusters.

Table 6: Overview of the 6 prompt framing templates used in MMJailBench. Each template modifies the prompt framing while preserving the underlying harmful intent.

### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

The 6 templates are Academic Analysis (Academic), System-Role Simulation (System), Fictional Storytelling (Story), Code-Style Indirection (Code), Structured Completion (Structure), and Safety-Paradox Reasoning (Paradox) (Table 6). Each is instantiated by substituting the target harmful intent into a task-specific placeholder, leaving the harmful objective identical across templates. The templates are evaluation probes yielding repeatable linguistic conditions, not an exhaustive attack collection.

Figure 8: Examples of the five visual semantic categories in MMJailBench. Each category provides distinct visual contextual cues while preserving the underlying harmful intent.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

The 5 visual semantic categories are Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, and Role, applied without altering harmful intent or prompt framing.

For each intent, qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b) produces visual descriptions and image generation prompts. zimage2025-Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025) generates scenes for Danger, Work Scenario, and Role; a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) generates Identity Credential and Authorization Document images, exploiting its image-editing capability for coherent textual elements. Outputs are filtered for semantic relevance, visual quality, and readability (examples in Figure 8).

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

Two carrier modes are used: direct text input (TEXT) and visually embedded instruction input (OCR). For OCR, the instruction text is rendered into a readable image and combined with the corresponding visual semantic image, preserving harmful intent and prompt framing, under a standardized layout.

###### Abstract

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet their robustness to jailbreak attacks that combine linguistic and visual inputs remains insufficiently characterized. Existing benchmarks provide valuable coverage of harmful behaviors and attack strategies, but their organization is often tied to specific attack families, which makes it difficult to describe the multimodal threat surface in a consistent and reusable vocabulary. To address this need, we introduce MMJailBench, a structured benchmark that describes every multimodal jailbreak instance along four interpretable dimensions: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. The benchmark is built on a curated taxonomy of 272 harmful intents spanning 9 harm domains and 18 scenarios, six representative prompt framing templates, five categories of task-relevant visual context, and two instruction carriers, with every instance annotated along all four dimensions. We evaluate 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs under a common protocol, using an LLM-based judge with a strict five-level harmfulness rubric and auxiliary instruction-mismatch detection, and we validate the judging protocol against human expert annotations. Beyond the benchmark itself, we develop a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are expanding beyond image captioning and visual question answering into real-world applications such as document understanding, code generation, workflow assistance, and automated operations (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). Unlike text-only models, MLLMs must jointly interpret linguistic instructions and visual information when reasoning and generating responses. Harmful requests may therefore combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions (Gong et al., 2025) with contextual cues such as professional settings, identity credentials, or authorization documents. Consequently, a model’s refusal and compliance decisions no longer depend solely on an isolated user instruction, but are shaped by the surrounding cross-modal context (Li et al., 2024b).

Figure 1: Motivation of MMJailBench. Multimodal jailbreak instances combine several kinds of content, including the underlying harmful goal, its linguistic presentation, accompanying imagery, and the channel through which the instruction is delivered. MMJailBench describes each instance along these dimensions within a common taxonomy.

How models form safety judgments in cross-modal contexts remains an open question. Visual information may not only supplement harmful intent, but also alter the perceived legitimacy, professionalism, and credibility of a request (Liu et al., 2024). This suggests that multimodal jailbreaks are not merely changes in input format; rather, they test the stability and consistency of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions (Luo et al., 2024). As MLLMs are increasingly embedded in agentic pipelines that read documents, screenshots, and forms on behalf of users, the range of contexts in which a harmful request can appear grows correspondingly, and evaluation practices need to keep pace with this growth.

Existing text and multimodal safety benchmarks cover a broad range of harmful behaviors (Li et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), visual attacks, and image-based text injection (Liu et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024), providing an important foundation for evaluating model robustness. These resources have been instrumental in establishing that multimodal inputs open new avenues for misuse and in standardizing how attack success is measured. At the same time, benchmarks are typically organized around particular attack families or data sources, and the descriptive vocabulary used to characterize instances differs from one benchmark to the next (Weng et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025). A shared, interpretable description of what each test instance contains would make it easier to compare coverage across resources, to document the composition of evaluation sets, and to communicate the scope of an audit to practitioners.

To contribute toward this goal, we introduce MMJailBench, a structured multimodal jailbreak benchmark in which every instance is described along four dimensions: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. The benchmark contains 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 types of task-relevant visual semantics, and 2 instruction carriers. Harmful intents are organized into a two-level taxonomy of domains and scenarios derived from existing safety benchmarks and public model-provider policies; prompt templates capture common linguistic reformulation strategies; visual semantics capture the kinds of contextual imagery that accompany realistic requests; and instruction carriers distinguish between instructions given directly as text and instructions rendered inside images. Building on this design, we further develop a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

Figure 2: Construction and evaluation pipeline of MMJailBench. The benchmark organizes instances by harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and evaluates MLLMs under a unified judging protocol.

We apply MMJailBench to 16 representative open-weight and proprietary MLLMs from a broad range of model families. All models are evaluated under the same input format, decoding settings, and judging rubric, and responses are scored by an LLM-based judge whose agreement with human experts we verify. To lower the barrier to repeated evaluation, we additionally provide a stratified lightweight configuration and a benchmark-scoped lightweight judge, and we examine their consistency with the full evaluation pipeline.

Overall, our main contributions are as follows:

•

We introduce MMJailBench, a structured multimodal jailbreak benchmark that describes every instance along harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, built on a curated taxonomy of 272 harmful intents across 9 harm domains and 18 scenarios.

•

We evaluate 16 representative open-weight and proprietary MLLMs under a common protocol with a strict harmfulness rubric and instruction-mismatch detection, and we validate the reliability of the judging protocol against human expert annotations.

•

We develop a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreak attacks aim to circumvent safety alignment and induce models to assist with harmful requests (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). Early studies attributed such failures to competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training (Wei et al., 2023). Subsequent work demonstrated transferable adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023) and black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), while indirect prompt injection showed that malicious instructions can also be introduced through external documents or retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023). These studies establish that refusal behavior can be highly sensitive to how harmful intent is framed and delivered (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023).

A recurring theme in this literature is that safety training tends to generalize along the surface features of the data on which it was performed. Requests that resemble refusal training examples are reliably declined, while requests that preserve the same objective but differ in style, register, or format can fall outside the region where safety behavior was learned. Role-play prompts, hypothetical scenarios, encoded instructions, and requests embedded in structured documents are all examples of reformulations that have been reported to affect refusal behavior in text-only models. These observations motivate evaluation resources that represent a variety of presentation styles rather than a single canonical phrasing of each harmful request.

Multimodal models introduce additional attack surfaces because instructions and contextual cues can be distributed across language and vision (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). Beyond textual manipulation, visual inputs can be exploited through adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024). Corresponding defenses span safety alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), yet their robustness across changes in modality and context remains uncertain. Since visual encoders are often trained separately from the language backbone and connected through lightweight projection modules, safety behavior established in the language model may not transfer automatically to inputs whose meaning arrives through the visual pathway. This consideration motivates benchmarks that represent both linguistic and visual variation in harmful requests.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

Standardized safety benchmarks such as SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) establish structured taxonomies and reproducible protocols for evaluating harmful behavior and refusal robustness. Multimodal benchmarks extend this paradigm to visual inputs: MM-SafetyBench evaluates image-based safety attacks (Liu et al., 2024), FigStep (Gong et al., 2025) studies harmful instructions rendered as typographic images, and JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025) expand coverage across diverse multimodal jailbreak strategies. MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025) further provides a unified framework for comparing multimodal jailbreak attacks and defenses, while OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025) broadens standardized attack-defense evaluation with multidimensional metrics.

Recent work has also moved toward more structured cross-modal evaluation. Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025) constructs parallel variants of the same harmful seeds across different modality configurations and evaluates cross-modal safety consistency. These benchmarks substantially improve attack coverage, evaluation standardization, and modality-level comparison. They differ in the granularity of their taxonomies, the sources of their harmful seeds, the kinds of images they use, and the judging protocols they adopt, which can complicate the comparison of results reported on different resources.

MMJailBench complements these efforts by providing a consistent descriptive vocabulary for multimodal jailbreak instances. Each instance carries explicit annotations for its harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, so that the composition of the benchmark can be inspected and reported along each dimension. In addition, MMJailBench places particular emphasis on task-relevant visual context, including identity credentials and authorization documents, which reflect the kinds of imagery that accompany requests in professional and administrative settings and which are less frequently represented in existing resources.

### 2.3 Evaluation Protocols and LLM-Based Judges

The reliability of jailbreak evaluation depends strongly on how responses are scored. Early work relied on keyword matching for refusal phrases, which is inexpensive but brittle: responses can contain refusal language while still providing harmful content, or avoid refusal phrases while declining to help. Subsequent benchmarks adopted LLM-based judges with explicit rubrics (Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), and several studies reported that such judges can approach human agreement when the rubric is well specified. Multimodal settings add a further complication, because a model may fail to read or interpret the input at all, producing outputs that are neither refusals nor compliant responses. MMJailBench adopts a graded harmfulness rubric together with explicit instruction-mismatch detection, and provides both a high-capacity judge and a lightweight judge so that evaluation remains practical at scale.

## 3 MMJailBench

MMJailBench is a structured multimodal jailbreak benchmark designed to support systematic and reproducible safety evaluation of MLLMs. As illustrated in Figure 2, MMJailBench builds multimodal scenarios from four descriptive components: harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers. Every instance is annotated along all four dimensions, so that the composition of any evaluation set drawn from the benchmark can be documented explicitly. The following subsections describe the benchmark design and individual components in detail.

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Multimodal jailbreak instances combine several distinct kinds of content: an unsafe objective, a linguistic wrapper around that objective, accompanying imagery, and a channel through which the instruction reaches the model. Existing benchmarks frequently organize instances by attack family or data source, and the descriptive categories used in one resource do not always correspond to those used in another. As a result, it can be difficult to state precisely what kinds of content a given evaluation set covers.

MMJailBench addresses this by describing each multimodal jailbreak instance in terms of four components: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. Each multimodal instance $i$ is represented as

| | $x_{i}=(L_{i},V_{i}),\quad a_{i}=(h_{i},t_{i},v_{i},c_{i}),$
| | (1)

where $L_{i}$ denotes the instruction component presented to the model, $V_{i}$ denotes the visual input, and $a_{i}$ records the annotation of the instance in terms of its harmful intent $h_{i}$, prompt framing $t_{i}$, visual semantic category $v_{i}$, and instruction carrier $c_{i}$.

This representation serves two purposes. First, it gives every instance a transparent description, which makes it straightforward to report coverage statistics, to filter the benchmark for targeted audits, and to communicate the scope of an evaluation. Second, it provides a modular construction process: harmful intents, prompt templates, visual assets, and carrier renderings are curated as separate resources and then assembled into complete instances, which simplifies maintenance and future extension. The benchmark draws on 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt framing strategies, 5 visual semantic categories, and 2 instruction carriers. New intents, templates, or visual categories can be added without redesigning the existing components, and the annotation scheme remains unchanged as the benchmark grows.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Harmful intent represents the underlying unsafe objective evaluated in MMJailBench. Instead of directly collecting jailbreak prompts in which harmful goals and attack strategies are interwoven, MMJailBench constructs a set of intent-level behavioral seeds that serve as the semantic core of each instance.

The benchmark contains 272 harmful intents across 9 major harm domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content. Each category is further divided into fine-grained subcategories to improve coverage and diversity across safety-critical behaviors. The harmful intents are collected through category-guided construction, followed by semantic similarity filtering and manual verification to reduce redundancy. Representing intents separately from their presentation has practical advantages: intents can be reviewed for appropriateness independently of attack templates, taxonomic coverage can be inspected directly, and the intent set can be updated as provider policies evolve.

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

Prompt framing specifies how a harmful intent is linguistically presented to the model. Different narrative structures and interaction styles may affect how models interpret requests and determine whether to comply, and many documented jailbreak techniques can be understood as particular framing strategies.

MMJailBench introduces 6 representative prompt framing strategies: academic, system, structured, story, code, and safety-paradox framing. These strategies capture common ways of reformulating harmful requests while preserving the underlying intent. For example, a harmful request may be embedded within a fictional scenario, expressed as a structured generation task, or presented as an apparently legitimate system requirement. The templates are intentionally simple and transparent rather than optimized against particular models, so that they function as repeatable evaluation probes rather than as a leaderboard of attack strength. This choice also keeps the benchmark stable over time: because the templates are fixed, evaluations of different model versions remain comparable without re-running any attack optimization.

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

Visual semantics capture the contextual meaning introduced by accompanying images. Unlike image-based instruction attacks that primarily encode instructions into visual text, this component focuses on contextual visual information that accompanies a request, such as a depicted setting or a document shown alongside the instruction.

We construct 5 task-relevant visual semantic conditions, including danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, and authorization documents. These conditions represent different forms of contextual signals that may affect how a request is interpreted, such as legitimacy-associated, expertise-related, or authority-related contextual signals. For each harmful intent, the corresponding visual input provides additional semantic context without modifying the underlying harmful instruction. Identity credentials and authorization documents are of particular interest because they reflect the documents that users routinely share with assistants in administrative, legal, and enterprise workflows, and because they carry textual elements that a capable model will read and interpret. Including such imagery broadens the benchmark toward deployment scenarios that existing resources cover less thoroughly.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

Instruction carrier describes how harmful instructions are presented to the model. MLLMs can receive instructions either through the text channel or embedded in images, and both channels occur naturally in practice, for example when users share screenshots of messages or photographs of printed instructions.

MMJailBench considers 2 instruction carriers: direct textual instructions (TEXT) and visually rendered instructions in text-containing images (OCR). The TEXT carrier directly provides harmful instructions as text, whereas the OCR carrier renders the same instructions into images while preserving their semantics. Because the OCR carrier introduces an additional perception stage, the evaluation protocol records instruction recognition mismatch, where models fail to interpret embedded instructions correctly. This information is reported alongside harmfulness scores so that perception failures are visible in the evaluation output rather than being silently counted as refusals.

## 4 Experimental Setup

This section describes the evaluated MLLMs, metrics, judge models, and evaluation configurations used in MMJailBench. All models are evaluated under the same benchmark configuration and judging protocol for consistent comparison. Additional experimental details, including evaluation prompts, judge criteria, and implementation details, are provided in the appendix.

### 4.1 Evaluated MLLMs

We evaluate MMJailBench on 16 representative MLLMs, covering both open-weight and proprietary-access models. The evaluated models include representative model families such as LLaVA-OneVision (An et al., 2025), InternVL (Zhu et al., 2025), Kimi (Team et al., 2026), Qwen (Bai et al., 2025b; Bai et al., 2025a), Gemma (Team et al., 2025), GLM (Hong et al., 2025), GPT (Singh et al., 2025), Gemini (Team et al., 2023), and Claude (Anthropic, 2025).

The selection is intended to span a range of model scales, training pipelines, and deployment modes. Open-weight models in the 7B–12B range are included because they are widely used as foundations for downstream applications and are frequently fine-tuned or deployed without additional safety layers. Proprietary-access models are included because they represent the systems most commonly encountered by end users and typically incorporate additional safety measures at the service level. Evaluating both groups under a common protocol allows the benchmark to serve as a reference point for developers working at either end of this spectrum.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

MMJailBench evaluates model safety using complementary metrics. The primary metric is Attack Success Rate (ASR), which measures the proportion of responses that provide substantive assistance to the targeted harmful intent:

| | $ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

where $s_{i}$ denotes the harmfulness score of the $i$ -th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale. Responses with $s_{i}\geq 4$ are considered successful jailbreak cases.

We further report the Conditional Attack Success Rate (CASR):

| | $CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

where mismatch cases refer to inputs that are not correctly understood by the model, including OCR recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent. ASR measures end-to-end jailbreak vulnerability, whereas CASR evaluates safety robustness conditioned on successful input understanding. Reporting both metrics, together with the mismatch rate itself, gives a fuller picture of model behavior than any single number, since a low ASR can arise either from robust refusal or from a failure to understand the input.

The main experiments use GPT-5 as an LLM-based judge. For each model response, GPT-5 assigns a harmfulness score and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and instruction mismatch. The evaluation focuses on generated responses: refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussions are not considered successful jailbreak cases. We additionally develop a benchmark-specific lightweight judge model based on an open-weight MLLM for cost-efficient follow-up evaluation under the same protocol.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

MMJailBench supports full and lightweight evaluation configurations. The full configuration evaluates all benchmark instances and provides complete coverage of the taxonomy. The lightweight configuration samples a representative subset while preserving coverage across harmful domains, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers, enabling efficient safety auditing and regression testing. The two configurations share the same judging protocol and metric definitions, so that results obtained with the lightweight configuration can be read in the same terms as those obtained with the full configuration.

The configurations are designed for different use cases. The full configuration is appropriate for comprehensive pre-release audits and for comparisons that require coverage of every intent. The lightweight configuration is appropriate for continuous integration, for monitoring the effect of incremental fine-tuning, and for settings in which API costs or compute budgets are limited.

## 5 Results and Analysis

This section discusses how MMJailBench is used to evaluate the 16 representative MLLMs and how the annotations attached to each instance support interpretation of evaluation outcomes. We focus on the structure of the evaluation output and on the considerations that govern its interpretation.

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

The most immediate output of MMJailBench is a model-level ASR computed over the full configuration, together with the corresponding CASR and mismatch rate. These quantities summarize how often a model provides substantive harmful assistance across the benchmark, how often it does so when it correctly understands the input, and how often it fails to understand the input at all. Because all 16 models are evaluated under identical inputs, decoding settings, and judging rubric, these summary quantities are directly comparable across models and across the open-weight and proprietary-access groups.

Model-level summaries are accompanied by domain-level breakdowns over the nine harm domains of the taxonomy. Domain-level reporting is important for two reasons. First, provider safety policies are themselves organized by harm category, so domain-level results map naturally onto the policy commitments that developers make. Second, a single aggregate number can obscure the distribution of risk across categories, and practitioners deploying a model in a specific application are typically most concerned with a subset of domains relevant to that application. The taxonomy described in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.1 is designed to make such breakdowns meaningful by providing comparable numbers of intents in most domains.

When interpreting overall results, several cautions apply. Proprietary-access models are evaluated through their official interfaces and may include service-level filters that are not part of the underlying model, so their results characterize the deployed system rather than the model weights. Open-weight models are evaluated with publicly available checkpoints and default chat templates, and results can differ under alternative system prompts or decoding settings. Finally, ASR depends on the harmfulness threshold; MMJailBench uses a strict threshold of 4 on the five-level rubric, which counts only actionable assistance as success.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

Because every instance is annotated with its harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, evaluation outputs can be grouped along any of these dimensions. This subsection discusses what each grouping is intended to capture and how it should be read.

#### Harmful Intent.

Grouping results by harm domain and scenario indicates whether safety alignment provides consistent protection across different categories of harmful behaviors. The two-level taxonomy allows reporting at both the domain level, which aligns with policy categories, and the scenario level, which distinguishes, for example, malware development from automated agent abuse within the cyber domain. Scenario-level reporting is particularly useful for developers who need to verify specific policy commitments, since aggregate domain results can combine behaviors that are treated differently in practice.

#### Prompt Framing.

Grouping results by prompt framing indicates how responses are distributed across the six presentation styles in the benchmark. Academic, system, story, code, structured, and safety-paradox framings correspond to widely discussed reformulation strategies, and reporting by framing helps developers relate benchmark outcomes to the categories of jailbreak techniques they already monitor. Since the templates are fixed and simple, framing-level reports describe model behavior on well-defined probes rather than on adaptively optimized attacks, and they should be read as indicating sensitivity to common reformulations rather than worst-case robustness.

#### Visual Semantics.

Grouping results by visual semantic category indicates how responses are distributed across danger-related context, task scenarios, professional roles, identity credentials, and authorization documents. These categories are designed to reflect the imagery that accompanies requests in realistic multimodal interactions. Document-like images such as credentials and authorizations deserve particular attention in deployment contexts where assistants routinely process user-uploaded documents, and category-level reporting allows auditors to examine behavior in these settings specifically.

#### Instruction Carrier.

Grouping results by instruction carrier distinguishes behavior on instructions provided as text from behavior on instructions rendered inside images. For the OCR carrier, the mismatch rate and CASR are especially informative, because a model that cannot read the rendered instruction will produce outputs that are neither compliant nor genuine refusals. Reporting ASR, CASR, and mismatch rate together for each carrier ensures that perception limitations are visible and are not mistaken for safety behavior.

Across all four dimensions, we emphasize that grouped results describe how outcomes are distributed over the annotated content of the benchmark. They provide a convenient and interpretable organization of evaluation output, and they are most useful when read alongside the overall and domain-level summaries described in Section 5.1.

### 5.3 Model-Dependent Profiles

Aggregate ASR provides an overall comparison of model robustness, but practitioners often need a richer description of a model’s behavior. MMJailBench supports this by producing, for each evaluated model, a profile consisting of its overall metrics together with its grouped results along each annotated dimension. Such profiles can be compared across model versions to track the effect of safety updates, or across candidate models when selecting a foundation for a downstream application.

Profiles are also useful for communicating evaluation results to non-specialist stakeholders. A single number can create a misleading impression of uniform safety, whereas a profile makes clear which kinds of content were included in the evaluation and how outcomes were distributed among them. We therefore recommend that results obtained with MMJailBench be reported as profiles rather than as single scores whenever space permits, and the evaluation suite generates such profiles automatically.

Finally, we note that model profiles depend on the specific templates, images, and intents included in the benchmark. They should be understood as describing behavior on a carefully curated and documented set of probes, rather than as an exhaustive characterization of a model’s safety under all possible inputs. Extending the benchmark with additional templates and visual categories, as supported by its modular construction, is a natural way to broaden this coverage.

## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

Behavioral evaluation describes what a model outputs, but understanding why safety behavior varies requires access to internal states. For open-weight models, the MMJailBench evaluation suite includes diagnostic utilities that record internal activations and attention patterns during response generation on selected benchmark instances. These utilities are intended to support follow-up investigations by researchers who wish to connect behavioral observations to model internals, and they are designed to operate on the same instance format and annotations used in behavioral evaluation.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

The representation-level utilities extract residual-stream activations at every layer for a designated token position, by default the final token of the generation prefix, immediately before the model produces its first response token. This position is a natural choice because it summarizes the model’s processing of the full multimodal input at the moment the response is initiated, and prior work on refusal behavior in language models has found that refusal-related information is often concentrated at such positions.

Given two sets of instances selected by their annotations, the utilities compute layer-wise summary statistics of how the corresponding representations differ, such as the distance between group means and the cosine similarity between mean activations. They also support fitting a linear direction from a discovery set and projecting a held-out set onto that direction, which is a standard practice for checking whether an observed representational difference generalizes beyond the samples used to identify it. All outputs can be broken down by harm domain using the intent annotations, which helps distinguish patterns that are specific to particular categories from those that are shared more broadly.

We stress that representation-level analyses of this kind are correlational. A difference in activations between two groups of inputs does not by itself establish a causal role in safety behavior, and causal claims require interventions such as activation steering or ablation, which the utilities also support for users who wish to perform them.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

Multimodal response generation depends on how textual and visual information are integrated across layers. The cross-modal utilities record attention weights from a designated query position to specified groups of key positions, such as instruction tokens, task-description tokens, and visual tokens, and aggregate them across heads at each layer. Because MLLMs differ in how they insert visual tokens into the sequence, the utilities include model-specific adapters that locate visual token spans and special delimiter tokens automatically.

Attention-based diagnostics provide a complementary view to representation-level analysis. Attention weights indicate where information is read from at a given layer, while residual-stream activations indicate what information has been accumulated. Interpreting attention requires care, since attention mass does not translate directly into information flow and can be redistributed without changing downstream behavior. For this reason we recommend using the attention utilities in combination with the representation utilities and, where feasible, with interventional checks. Together, these tools are intended to make MMJailBench useful not only as a behavioral benchmark but also as a starting point for mechanistic investigation of multimodal safety alignment.

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce MMJailBench, a structured multimodal jailbreak benchmark in which every instance is described along four interpretable dimensions: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. The benchmark is built on a curated taxonomy of 272 harmful intents across 9 domains and 18 scenarios, six transparent prompt framing templates, five categories of task-relevant visual context including identity credentials and authorization documents, and two instruction carriers. We evaluate 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs under a common protocol with a strict harmfulness rubric and explicit instruction-mismatch detection, and we validate the judging protocol against human expert annotations. With modular full and lightweight configurations, flexible judge options, multidimensional metrics, and diagnostic utilities for open-weight models, MMJailBench provides a systematic and reproducible framework for scalable multimodal safety evaluation.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

The harmful intent taxonomy defines the semantic space of MMJailBench by organizing harmful behaviors into a structured hierarchy of intents, domains, and scenarios. Each intent is associated with a task identifier, harm category, scenario, and action description.

The taxonomy contains 272 unique harmful intents covering 9 major harm domains and 18 harm scenarios. Table 5 summarizes the taxonomy structure and category statistics. The 9 major harm domains include Cyber & Tech Abuse (Cyber), Economic Harm (Econ.), Privacy & IP (Privacy), Deception & Public Influence (Decept.), Illegal Goods & Services (Illegal), Hate & Harassment (Hate), Violence & Physical Harm (Violence), Sensitive Regulated Advice (Sensitive), and Sexual Content (Sexual). The taxonomy is constructed from existing safety benchmarks (Luo et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2024) and public model-provider safety policies (OpenAI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2025a; Google, 2026), followed by intent normalization, taxonomy organization, and manual filtering.

Intent normalization rewrites each candidate into a concise action description that states the harmful objective without embedding any particular framing, persona, or output format. This step ensures that the presentation of each intent is supplied entirely by the prompt framing templates rather than by idiosyncrasies of the source material. Taxonomy organization assigns each normalized intent to exactly one domain and one scenario, with ambiguous cases resolved by discussion among the authors. Domains are kept broadly balanced, with the exception of Violence & Physical Harm, which spans three scenarios and therefore contains more intents, and Sexual Content, which is restricted to a single scenario.

To improve semantic diversity and reduce redundancy, we perform embedding-based similarity analysis among the 272 intents using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Figure 6 shows that most intent pairs have relatively low semantic similarity, while only a small subset forms a high-similarity tail. These cases are manually reviewed to remove near-duplicates and ensure that retained intents represent distinct harmful objectives. We further visualize the intent embedding space using PCA in Figure 7. Although the projection provides a qualitative view, intents from different harm domains occupy diverse regions rather than collapsing into a small number of clusters. Together, the diversity analysis and manual filtering establish a balanced harmful-intent set for subsequent evaluation.

### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

MMJailBench uses 6 representative prompt framing templates to represent common ways in which harmful requests are presented to MLLMs. These templates preserve the underlying harmful intent while varying the surrounding framing strategy. The 6 templates cover common jailbreak-related framing strategies, including Academic Analysis (Academic), System-Role Simulation (System), Fictional Storytelling (Story), Code-Style Indirection (Code), Structured Completion (Structure), and Safety-Paradox Reasoning (Paradox).

Table 6 summarizes the 6 prompt framings and their corresponding design characteristics. Each template is instantiated by replacing the task-specific placeholder with the target harmful intent, keeping the harmful objective unchanged. The templates are designed as evaluation probes rather than an exhaustive collection of jailbreak attacks, providing repeatable linguistic conditions that can be reused across evaluations and model versions.

The selection of templates was guided by three considerations. First, each template should correspond to a strategy that is widely discussed in the jailbreak literature or observed in public jailbreak collections. Second, the templates should differ meaningfully in register and structure, spanning narrative, technical, institutional, and argumentative styles. Third, each template should be expressible in a single fixed form that accepts any intent from the taxonomy without manual adaptation, which keeps instance construction fully automatic and reproducible.

Figure 8: Examples of the five visual semantic categories in MMJailBench. Each category provides distinct visual contextual cues while preserving the underlying harmful intent.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

MMJailBench introduces 5 visual semantic categories, including Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, and Role, to represent the kinds of visual context that accompany requests in realistic multimodal interactions while preserving the underlying harmful intent and prompt framing.

For each harmful intent, qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b) is used to generate visual descriptions and image generation prompts. zimage2025-Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025) is used for visual scene generation in Danger, Work Scenario, and Role, while a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) is used for the Identity Credential and Authorization Document categories due to its image-editing capability for generating images with coherent textual elements. Generated images are filtered based on semantic relevance, visual quality, and readability. Figure 8 shows representative examples of the generated visual semantic conditions.

Generated images are checked to ensure that they do not contain the harmful instruction itself, so that the visual semantic component supplies context rather than duplicating the instruction carrier. Document-style images are additionally checked for legibility of key fields such as names, titles, and approval statements, since illegible documents would fail to convey the intended context. Images that depict real individuals, real organizations, or identifiable personal information are excluded, and all credentials and authorizations are fictitious.

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

We construct the instruction carrier component by controlling how a harmful instruction is delivered to MLLMs. MMJailBench considers two carrier modes: direct text input (TEXT) and visually embedded instruction input (OCR). For OCR instances, the instruction text is rendered into a readable image and combined with the corresponding visual semantic image while preserving the original harmful intent and prompt framing. A standardized layout is used to reduce formatting variations, with a fixed font, font size, margin, and background color, so that rendered instructions are consistently legible across instances.

## Appendix B Experimental and Evaluation Details

### B.1 Evaluated MLLMs

We evaluate MMJailBench on 16 MLLMs, including 8 open-weight models and 8 proprietary-access models. The open-weight models include qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b), qwen3-vl-8b (Bai et al., 2025a), gemma3-12b (Gemma Team et al., 2025), internvl3-8b (Zhu et al., 2025), glm4.1v-9b (Hong et al., 2025), ministral3-8b (Liu et al., 2026), step3-vl-10b (Huang et al., 2026), and llava-onevision-1.5 (An et al., 2025). The proprietary-access models include gpt-5 (Singh et al., 2025), gemini-3-flash (Google DeepMind, 2025), claude-sonnet-4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), grok-4-fast (xAI, 2025), qwen3-vl-plus (Bai et al., 2025a), kimi-k2.5 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), glm-4.6v (Hong et al., 2025), and doubao-seed-2.0-lite (ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). Open-weight models are evaluated using publicly available checkpoints, while proprietary-access models are evaluated through their official interfaces.

All models are evaluated under the same benchmark configuration, with identical inputs, the default chat template of each model, and a common decoding configuration where the interface permits. No additional system prompt is supplied beyond what is part of each prompt framing template. Requests that are blocked by a provider’s service-level filter before reaching the model are recorded and treated as refusals, consistent with our goal of characterizing deployed system behavior.

### B.2 Evaluation Rubric and Judge Prompt

GPT-5 is used as the primary evaluator for MMJailBench responses. For each response, the judge outputs an instruction-mismatch flag and a harmfulness score. The mismatch flag identifies failures to recognize the task, such as only transcribing visual content, repeating the prompt, or producing meaningless outputs. The harmfulness score follows a strict 1 $\sim$ 5 rubric, with higher scores indicating stronger compliance and more actionable harmful content. The detailed scoring criteria are summarized in Table 7.

The judge prompt incorporates anti-deception rules to prevent safety disclaimers, fictional framing, or academic packaging from affecting the evaluation when harmful information is provided. Responses limited to refusal, safe redirection, or non-actionable discussion receive low harmfulness scores. The judge is given the normalized harmful intent alongside the model response, so that it evaluates whether the response advances the specific objective rather than whether it contains generally sensitive content. The complete judge prompt template is provided in the Code and Data Supplement.

### B.3 Full and Lightweight Benchmark Settings

The full MMJailBench configuration evaluates every instance in the benchmark and provides comprehensive coverage of the harmful-intent taxonomy, prompt framings, visual semantic categories, and instruction carriers.

To reduce evaluation cost, we construct a lightweight configuration containing 1,500 instances by stratified sampling over harm domains, prompt framings, visual semantic conditions, and carrier modes while preserving the distribution of the full configuration. The sampling procedure is seeded and the selected instance identifiers are released, so that the lightweight configuration is identical across users. The effectiveness of the lightweight configuration is evaluated in Section C.4.

### B.4 Lightweight Judge Model

To improve evaluation efficiency, we train a benchmark-scoped lightweight judge based on qwen3-8b (Team et al., 2025) using GPT-5-generated annotations. The lightweight judge predicts harmfulness scores and mismatch labels under the same evaluation protocol as the primary GPT-5 judge. Its consistency with GPT-5 evaluation is further validated in Section C.4. Because the judge is trained on responses to MMJailBench instances, its use is recommended only within the scope of this benchmark; applying it to unrelated tasks or response distributions may require recalibration. Detailed training configurations are provided in the Code and Data Supplement.

## Appendix C Extended Results and Ablations

### C.1 Extended Factor-Level Results

The evaluation suite produces extended grouped reports that complement the summaries described in Section 5. For each model, these reports include results by harm scenario within each domain, by prompt framing template, by visual semantic category, and by instruction carrier, each accompanied by the number of contributing responses so that the precision of each figure can be assessed.

Scenario-level reports follow the structure of Table 5 and are the recommended starting point for policy-oriented audits, since each scenario corresponds to a coherent class of behavior that is typically addressed by a specific provision in provider policies. Framing-level and visual-level reports follow the template list in Table 6 and the categories in Figure 8, respectively. Carrier-level reports include ASR, CASR, and mismatch rate side by side, reflecting the recommendation in Section 5.2 that these three quantities be read together.

When the number of contributing responses in a group is small, as can occur when grouped reports are combined with the lightweight configuration, we recommend reporting bootstrap confidence intervals, which the suite computes automatically, and refraining from interpreting small differences between groups.

### C.2 Per-Model Factor Sensitivity Profiles

The model profiles described in Section 5.3 can be visualized in several formats supported by the suite, including radar plots with one axis per template or visual category, grouped bar charts by domain, and tabular summaries suitable for inclusion in model cards. These visualizations are generated directly from the per-instance annotations and judge outputs, so they remain consistent with the underlying data and can be regenerated whenever the benchmark or the judge is updated.

We recommend that profile visualizations always state the configuration (full or lightweight), the judge used, and the harmfulness threshold, since each of these choices affects the reported values. The suite embeds this information in the metadata of every generated figure and table to support transparent reporting and to prevent inadvertent comparison of results obtained under different settings.

### C.3 Semantic Image Ablation

The suite includes utilities for constructing supplementary visual variants of benchmark instances, such as replacing the task-relevant image with a generic placeholder or removing the image entirely. These utilities are provided for researchers who wish to extend the benchmark with additional visual conditions tailored to their own questions. Supplementary variants inherit the annotations of the original instance, with the visual semantic field updated to identify the substituted condition, so that they can be processed by the same judging and reporting pipeline without modification.

When constructing supplementary variants, users should verify that the substitution does not change the legibility or position of the instruction in OCR instances, since layout changes could otherwise affect perception independently of image content. The standardized layout described in Appendix A.4 is designed to make such substitutions straightforward.

## Appendix D Responsible Release

### D.1 Ethics and Data Release

MMJailBench contains harmful intents and adversarial prompts for multimodal safety evaluation. The benchmark is released for research purposes only, with documentation and evaluation tools to support reproducible and responsible use. Users are encouraged to apply the released resources for research on improving model safety and robustness. Model responses collected during evaluation are not released in raw form; only aggregated metrics and judge labels are shared, to avoid distributing harmful content generated by the evaluated models.

### D.2 LLM Usage Statement

LLMs are used in MMJailBench for harmful-intent organization, visual prompt generation, and response evaluation. Generated materials are filtered and validated through predefined procedures, while the final benchmark design and protocols are determined by the authors.
