## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

From matched MMJailBench instances we build a diagnostic subset centered on authority-document scenarios and probe layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention in gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

We take residual-stream activations at the final generation-prefix token (Figure 4). Authority–danger representation divergence grows with depth, with the steepest rise at layer 42 (Figure 4(a)).

An authority-minus-danger direction is fit on discovery samples and applied, fixed, to held-out pairs. Authority-document contexts are clearly displaced along it (Figure 4(b)), and the shift is positive in every harm domain (Figure 4(c)), indicating a shared higher-layer pattern across diverse harmful objectives.

Figure 4: Representation-level diagnostics of gemma3-12b under authority-document and danger-image contexts, by layer and harm domain.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

We measure attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5). Layer-wise patterns differ between authority-document and danger-image contexts. At the representation-sensitive layer, authority-document contexts place lower attention mass on both token sets. Together with the representation displacement, this indicates a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention at response initiation, consistent with elevated susceptibility under authority-related visual contexts.

Figure 5: Cross-modal interaction diagnostics in gemma3-12b: layer-wise attention to harm-related textual tokens and visual tokens under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench analyzes multimodal jailbreak vulnerability through controlled variation of harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, prompt framing introduces the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability through contextual cues, instruction carriers act model-dependently, and harmful intents expose category-specific patterns; internal diagnostics show associated representation and cross-modal interaction patterns. Modular full and lightweight configurations, flexible judge options, and multidimensional metrics make MMJailBench a systematic, reproducible framework for scalable multimodal safety evaluation.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

The taxonomy is a hierarchy of intents, domains, and scenarios; each intent carries a task identifier, harm category, scenario, and action description. Pairwise similarity among the 272 intents is computed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). ### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

The 6 templates are Academic Analysis (Academic), System-Role Simulation (System), Fictional Storytelling (Story), Code-Style Indirection (Code), Structured Completion (Structure), and Safety-Paradox Reasoning (Paradox) (Table 6). Each is instantiated by substituting the target intent into a task-specific placeholder, leaving the harmful objective unchanged across templates. The templates are repeatable evaluation probes, not an exhaustive attack collection.

Figure 8: Examples of the five visual semantic categories in MMJailBench.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

The 5 visual categories are Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, and Role, each holding intent and prompt framing fixed. For each intent, qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b) produces visual descriptions and image-generation prompts. zimage2025-Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025) renders Danger, Work Scenario, and Role scenes; a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) handles Identity Credential and Authorization Document, using its image-editing capability to produce coherent embedded text. Images are filtered for semantic relevance, visual quality, and readability (examples in Figure 8).

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

Carriers are TEXT (direct text input) and OCR (visually embedded instruction input). For OCR, the instruction text is rendered into a readable image and composited with the corresponding visual semantic image under a standardized layout, preserving intent and prompt framing and limiting formatting variation between the two modes.

### B.2 Evaluation Rubric and Judge Prompt

GPT-5 outputs, per response, an instruction-mismatch flag and a harmfulness score. The flag marks task-recognition failures such as transcribing visual content only, repeating the prompt, or producing meaningless output. The score follows the strict 1 $\sim$ 5 rubric of Table 7. The judge prompt includes anti-deception rules so that safety disclaimers, fictional framing, or academic packaging do not lower the score when harmful information is provided; refusal, safe redirection, and non-actionable discussion score low. The full prompt template is in the Code and Data Supplement.

### B.3 Full and Lightweight Benchmark Settings

The full configuration is the complete Cartesian product of 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carrier modes, i.e., 16,320 instances per model. The lightweight configuration has 1,500 instances, stratified-sampled over harm domains, prompt framings, visual semantic conditions, and carrier modes to preserve the full factor distribution; it is validated in Section C.4.

### B.4 Lightweight Judge Model

A benchmark-scoped lightweight judge is fine-tuned from qwen3-8b (Team et al., 2025) on GPT-5-generated annotations to predict harmfulness scores and mismatch labels under the GPT-5 protocol. Agreement with GPT-5 is reported in Section C.4; training configurations are in the Code and Data Supplement.

###### Abstract

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet the determinants of their jailbreak behavior remain poorly characterized. Existing benchmarks construct fixed prompt-image instances in which harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier co-occur. We introduce MMJailBench, a benchmark built as the full Cartesian product of these four factors over a shared set of intents, so that every condition is matched against every other on identical seeds. Large-scale evaluation across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs yields heterogeneous, model-dependent vulnerability profiles. ASR varies markedly across harm domains; prompt framing produces the widest ASR range of any factor; task-relevant visual semantics raise ASR, most strongly for authority-like cues; and visually rendered instructions do not consistently exceed direct textual instructions in ASR. Diagnostic analyses on gemma3-12b identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. We release a modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

MLLMs now operate well beyond image captioning and visual question answering, in document understanding, code generation, workflow assistance, and automated operations (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). Their outputs are conditioned jointly on linguistic instructions and visual inputs, and harmful requests can combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions (Gong et al., 2025) with contextual cues such as professional settings, identity credentials, or authorization documents. Refusal and compliance are therefore functions of the full cross-modal context rather than of an isolated instruction (Li et al., 2024b).

Figure 1: Motivation of MMJailBench. Existing multimodal jailbreak benchmarks entangle multiple factors within fixed instances, limiting factor-level diagnosis. MMJailBench factorizes these factors and constructs a controlled evaluation space for fine-grained analysis.

Visual input can supply harmful content, but it can also modulate the perceived legitimacy, professionalism, and credibility of a request, so that one underlying intent elicits divergent refusal or compliance behavior across contexts (Liu et al., 2024). Multimodal jailbreaks thus probe the stability and consistency of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions (Luo et al., 2024), not merely robustness to an alternative input format.

Text and multimodal safety benchmarks cover a broad range of harmful behaviors (Li et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), visual attacks, and image-based text injection (Liu et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024). Each typically instantiates a harmful task as a fixed prompt-image pair that jointly encodes harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and reports attack success rate over that test set. Such scores measure aggregate vulnerability on the instance distribution, but do not separate contributions from linguistic framing, visual context, delivery modality, or domain-concentrated weaknesses (Weng et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025), as illustrated in Figure 1.

MMJailBench parameterizes instances by harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and evaluates their systematic combinations under matched comparisons. It comprises 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 types of task-relevant visual semantics, and 2 instruction carriers, yielding a structured, directly comparable evaluation space that supports both overall vulnerability measurement and factor-level attribution. On top of this design we provide a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

Figure 2: Construction and evaluation pipeline of MMJailBench. The benchmark factorizes harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and evaluates MLLMs under controlled multimodal jailbreak configurations.

Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, vulnerability is uneven across harm domains, with cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation highest. Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation: at fixed intent, narrative structure and output requirements substantially change refusal and compliance. Task-relevant visual semantics systematically weaken refusal, with authorization documents and identity credentials producing the largest effects, consistent with over-reliance on visually conveyed legitimacy and credibility. Instruction-carrier effects are highly model-dependent, and visually rendered instructions do not consistently increase susceptibility relative to direct text. Representation- and attention-level diagnostics on a representative open-weight model identify vulnerability-associated internal patterns.

Overall, our main contributions are as follows:

•

We introduce MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark that incorporates harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier into a unified controlled design, enabling fine-grained analysis and factor-level attribution of multimodal jailbreak vulnerabilities.

•

We conduct large-scale evaluations across 16 representative open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, revealing uneven jailbreak vulnerabilities across harm domains, the dominant role of prompt framing, the refusal-weakening effect of authority-like visual cues, and the model-dependent effect of instruction carriers. Diagnostic analyses on a representative open-weight model further identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions.

•

We develop a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics, enabling reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreak attacks circumvent safety alignment to elicit assistance with harmful requests (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). Early analyses attributed these failures to competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training (Wei et al., 2023). Later work introduced transferable adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023), black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), and indirect prompt injection through external documents or retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023). Collectively these results show refusal to be highly sensitive to how harmful intent is framed and delivered (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023).

In MLLMs, instructions and contextual cues may be distributed across language and vision (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), exposing additional surfaces: adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024). Defenses span safety alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), with uncertain robustness under shifts in modality and context; in particular, identical harmful intent may receive different safety treatment under different linguistic or visual contexts.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) establish structured taxonomies and reproducible protocols for harmful-behavior and refusal evaluation. On the multimodal side, MM-SafetyBench evaluates image-based safety attacks (Liu et al., 2024), FigStep (Gong et al., 2025) renders harmful instructions as typographic images, and JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025) broaden coverage of multimodal jailbreak strategies. MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025) offers a unified framework for comparing multimodal jailbreak attacks and defenses, and OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025) extends standardized attack-defense evaluation with multidimensional metrics.

Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025) constructs parallel variants of the same harmful seeds across modality configurations to measure cross-modal safety consistency. These efforts advance attack coverage, standardization, and modality-level comparison, but do not independently manipulate the linguistic and semantic factors that jointly shape safety decisions within matched multimodal interactions. MMJailBench varies prompt framing, task-relevant visual semantics, and instruction carrier over matched harmful intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

MMJailBench (Figure 2) constructs matched multimodal scenarios by systematically varying harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers within a unified evaluation space.

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Prior multimodal jailbreak benchmarks are organized around predefined attack instances or modality variations, in which harmful intent, linguistic formulation, visual context, and instruction presentation are jointly encoded per evaluation item.

MMJailBench decomposes an instance into harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. Given a harmful intent $h$ , a prompt framing strategy $t$ , a visual semantic condition $v$ , and an instruction carrier $c$ , each multimodal instance is represented as

| | $x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),$
| | (1)

where $L(h,t,c)$ denotes the instruction component generated from harmful intent $h$ , prompt framing $t$ , and instruction carrier $c$ , while $V(h,v)$ denotes the visual input associated with harmful intent $h$ and visual semantics $v$ .

The benchmark contains 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt framing strategies, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carriers, and their Cartesian product yields 16,320 controlled multimodal jailbreak instances. The same instance set is applied to every model and every harm category.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Harmful intents are intent-level behavioral seeds rather than collected jailbreak prompts, which would bind each harmful goal to a specific attack strategy; each seed remains fixed while the remaining factors vary.

The 272 intents span 9 major harm domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content, each subdivided into fine-grained subcategories. Intents are obtained by category-guided construction, then semantic-similarity filtering and manual verification to reduce redundancy (Appendix A.1).

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

Prompt framing determines the linguistic presentation of a fixed harmful intent, i.e., its narrative structure and interaction style.

MMJailBench uses 6 framing strategies: academic, system, structured, story, code, and safety-paradox. They reproduce common reformulations of harmful requests—embedding in fictional scenarios, casting as structured generation, or presentation as an apparently legitimate system requirement—while preserving intent (Appendix A.2).

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

Visual semantics denote the contextual meaning carried by the accompanying image. Unlike image-based instruction attacks, which encode the instruction as visual text, this factor leaves the harmful instruction unchanged and supplies additional semantic context per intent.

We define 5 task-relevant conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, and authorization documents, spanning legitimacy-associated, expertise-related, and authority-related signals. Control conditions with irrelevant or non-semantic images are used in diagnostic evaluations (Section 5.2, Appendix C.3).

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

The instruction carrier is the modality through which the instruction itself is presented, holding intent fixed.

MMJailBench considers 2 instruction carriers: direct textual instructions (TEXT) and visually rendered instructions in text-containing images (OCR). TEXT supplies the instruction as text; OCR renders the same instruction into an image with semantics preserved. Because OCR adds a perception stage, we record instruction recognition mismatch, i.e., failure to correctly interpret embedded instructions, and use it in CASR (Section 4.2).

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

The primary metric is Attack Success Rate (ASR):

| | $ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

where $s_{i}$ denotes the harmfulness score of the $i$ -th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale (Table 7). Responses with $s_{i}\geq 4$ are considered successful jailbreak cases.

For carrier analysis we additionally report the Conditional Attack Success Rate (CASR):

| | $CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

where $N_{mismatch}$ counts inputs not correctly understood by the model, comprising OCR recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent. ASR is end-to-end; CASR is conditioned on successful input understanding.

GPT-5 serves as the judge for all main results, assigning to each response a harmfulness score and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and instruction mismatch. Only generated content is judged; refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussion do not count as success. A benchmark-specific lightweight judge built on an open-weight MLLM is provided for follow-up evaluation under the same protocol (Appendix B.4).

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

The full configuration covers all instances and supports model-, domain-, and factor-level comparison. The lightweight configuration is a subset preserving coverage over harmful domains, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers, intended for efficient safety auditing and regression testing (Appendix B.3). Unless otherwise specified, all reported results use the full configuration.

## 5 Results and Analysis

Results cover the 16 MLLMs at three levels: overall vulnerability, factor-level effects, and per-model profiles.

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

Figure 3 and Table 1 report model-level ASR across controlled multimodal conditions and harm domains under the full configuration. Under identical configurations, average ASR ranges from 2.17% (GPT-5) to 78.38% (GLM-4.6V). Models of comparable multimodal capability can differ sharply in vulnerability, so general capability is not a proxy for jailbreak robustness.

Across harmful objectives, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally attain higher ASR, whereas categories such as physical harm are comparatively lower; current alignment does not provide uniform protection across objectives.

Figure 3: Model-level vulnerability profiles across prompt framing and visual semantic factors. Each radar plot shows ASR variation under controlled factor changes, revealing model-specific sensitivity patterns.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

We analyze each of harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier with the remaining conditions held fixed.

#### Harmful Intent.

Per Table 1, ASR varies substantially across harm domains: cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks are generally higher across models, while physical harm and sensitive content categories tend to be lower. Aggregate scores therefore conceal domain-specific weaknesses, which explicit intent modeling exposes.

#### Prompt Framing.

Prompt framing yields the largest variation among the evaluated factors. Sensitivity patterns differ across models (Figure 3(a)), but story, structured, and academic framings generally attain higher ASR, and system-style and safety-paradox framings lower. The gap between the most and least vulnerable strategies exceeds 40 percentage points, so MLLM behavior depends on interaction structure and linguistic presentation as well as on the intent itself.

### 5.3 Model-Dependent Profiles

Table 4 reports, per model, the ASR range induced by each factor. Several models are highly sensitive to prompt reframing, with $\Delta$ Prompt exceeding 80 percentage points, while others are more sensitive to instruction carrier changes. ## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

We construct a diagnostic subset of matched MMJailBench instances emphasizing authority-document scenarios, and analyze layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention in gemma3-12b under authority-document versus danger-image contexts.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Figure 4 analyzes residual-stream representations of the final generation-prefix token. Divergence between authority and danger conditions grows with depth, rising most sharply at layer 42 (Figure 4(a)), so the two visual contexts become increasingly separated in higher-layer representations before response generation.

We fit an authority-minus-danger direction on discovery samples and project held-out pairs onto the fixed direction. Authority-document contexts are clearly displaced along it (Figure 4(b)), and the shift is positive in every harm domain (Figure 4(c)), indicating a shared higher-layer representation pattern associated with authority cues across diverse harmful objectives.

Figure 4: Representation-level diagnostics of gemma3-12b under authority-document and danger-image contexts. Authority-related visual cues exhibit distinct representation patterns across layers and harm domains.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

We measure attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and to special visual tokens across layers (Figure 5), which shows distinct layer-wise profiles under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

At the representation-sensitive layer, authority-document contexts allocate lower attention mass to both harm-related task-label tokens and visual tokens. Together with the representation displacement, this is consistent with authority cues inducing a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention at response initiation, providing an internal account of the elevated susceptibility under authority-related visual contexts.

Figure 5: Cross-modal interaction diagnostics in gemma3-12b. Attention allocation to harm-related textual tokens and visual tokens varies across layers under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench evaluates multimodal jailbreak vulnerability under controlled variation of harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, prompt framing introduces the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability through contextual cues, instruction carriers have model-dependent effects, and harmful intents show category-specific patterns. Diagnostics on gemma3-12b locate vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. Full and lightweight configurations, flexible judge options, and multidimensional metrics make the framework systematic, reproducible, and scalable for multimodal safety evaluation.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

The taxonomy is a hierarchy of intents, domains, and scenarios; each intent carries a task identifier, harm category, scenario, and action description.

It contains 272 unique intents over 9 major harm domains and 18 harm scenarios (Table 5): Cyber & Tech Abuse (Cyber), Economic Harm (Econ.), Privacy & IP (Privacy), Deception & Public Influence (Decept.), Illegal Goods & Services (Illegal), Hate & Harassment (Hate), Violence & Physical Harm (Violence), Sensitive Regulated Advice (Sensitive), and Sexual Content (Sexual). Sources are existing safety benchmarks (Luo et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2024) and public model-provider safety policies (OpenAI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2025a; Google, 2026), followed by intent normalization, taxonomy organization, and manual filtering.

Pairwise semantic similarity among the 272 intents is computed with the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Most pairs have relatively low similarity, with a small high-similarity tail (Figure 6); tail pairs are manually reviewed and near-duplicates removed so that retained intents correspond to distinct harmful objectives. A PCA projection of the embedding space (Figure 7) shows, qualitatively, that intents from different domains occupy diverse regions rather than collapsing into a few clusters.

### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

The 6 templates are Academic Analysis (Academic), System-Role Simulation (System), Fictional Storytelling (Story), Code-Style Indirection (Code), Structured Completion (Structure), and Safety-Paradox Reasoning (Paradox), summarized in Table 6. Each is instantiated by substituting the target harmful intent into a task-specific placeholder, leaving the harmful objective identical across templates. The templates are evaluation probes yielding repeatable linguistic conditions, not an exhaustive collection of jailbreak attacks.

Figure 8: Examples of the five visual semantic categories in MMJailBench. Each category provides distinct visual contextual cues while preserving the underlying harmful intent.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

The 5 visual semantic categories are Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, and Role; each preserves the underlying harmful intent and prompt framing.

For each intent, qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b) produces visual descriptions and image generation prompts. zimage2025-Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025) generates scenes for Danger, Work Scenario, and Role; a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) generates Identity Credential and Authorization Document images, using its image-editing capability to produce coherent textual elements. Outputs are filtered on semantic relevance, visual quality, and readability. Representative examples appear in Figure 8.

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

TEXT supplies the instruction directly as input text. For OCR, the instruction text is rendered into a readable image and combined with the corresponding visual semantic image, preserving the original harmful intent and prompt framing, under a standardized layout that limits formatting variation between the two carriers.

### B.2 Evaluation Rubric and Judge Prompt

GPT-5 outputs, per response, an instruction-mismatch flag and a harmfulness score. The mismatch flag marks task-recognition failures, including mere transcription of visual content, prompt repetition, and meaningless output. The harmfulness score follows the strict 1 $\sim$ 5 rubric of Table 7, higher scores indicating stronger compliance and more actionable harmful content.

The judge prompt includes anti-deception rules so that safety disclaimers, fictional framing, or academic packaging do not lower the score when harmful information is actually provided; refusal, safe redirection, or non-actionable discussion receive low scores. The full judge prompt template is in the Code and Data Supplement.

### B.3 Full and Lightweight Benchmark Settings

The full configuration is the complete Cartesian product of 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carrier modes, i.e., 16,320 instances per model.

The lightweight configuration contains 1,500 instances drawn by stratified sampling over harm domains, prompt framings, visual semantic conditions, and carrier modes, preserving the factor distribution of the full configuration. Its agreement with the full configuration is reported in Section C.4.

### B.4 Lightweight Judge Model

The lightweight judge is a benchmark-scoped model trained from qwen3-8b (Team et al., 2025) on GPT-5-generated annotations. It predicts harmfulness scores and mismatch labels under the protocol of the GPT-5 judge; agreement is reported in Section C.4, and training configurations are in the Code and Data Supplement.

###### Abstract

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet how different factors shape their jailbreak vulnerabilities remains poorly understood. Existing benchmarks often couple harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier within individual jailbreak instances. We introduce MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark that systematically varies and combines these factors under controlled configurations. Large-scale evaluations across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs reveal highly heterogeneous and model-dependent vulnerability profiles. Jailbreak vulnerability varies markedly across harm domains. Prompt framing emerges as the dominant source of variation, task-relevant visual semantics systematically increase jailbreak susceptibility with authority-like cues exposing particularly pronounced vulnerabilities, and visually rendered instructions do not consistently increase jailbreak susceptibility relative to direct textual instructions. Diagnostic analyses on a representative open-weight model identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. We also release a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are expanding beyond image captioning and visual question answering into document understanding, code generation, workflow assistance, and automated operations (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). MLLMs jointly interpret linguistic instructions and visual information when reasoning and generating responses, so a harmful request may combine direct textual or visually rendered instructions (Gong et al., 2025) with contextual cues such as professional settings, identity credentials, or authorization documents, and refusal and compliance are jointly shaped by the surrounding cross-modal context (Li et al., 2024b).

Figure 1: Motivation of MMJailBench. Existing multimodal jailbreak benchmarks entangle multiple factors within fixed instances. MMJailBench factorizes these factors and constructs a controlled evaluation space.

Visual information may not only supplement harmful intent but also alter the perceived legitimacy, professionalism, and credibility of a request, so that the same underlying intent elicits different refusal or compliance behaviors across contexts (Liu et al., 2024). Multimodal jailbreaks thereby probe the stability and consistency of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions (Luo et al., 2024), rather than constituting mere changes in input format.

Existing text and multimodal safety benchmarks cover a broad range of harmful behaviors (Li et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), visual attacks, and image-based text injection (Liu et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024). These benchmarks typically construct fixed prompt-image pairs per harmful task, jointly encoding harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier within a single test instance, and report attack success rates over the resulting test set (Weng et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025); see Figure 1.

MMJailBench incorporates harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier into a unified controlled design using systematic combinations and matched comparisons. It contains 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 types of task-relevant visual semantics, and 2 instruction carriers. On top of it, we develop a modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics.

Figure 2: Construction and evaluation pipeline of MMJailBench. The benchmark factorizes harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, and evaluates MLLMs under controlled multimodal jailbreak configurations.

We evaluate 16 representative open-weight and proprietary MLLMs. Cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation exhibit greater overall vulnerability. Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation: with harmful intent held fixed, narrative structure and output requirements substantially alter refusal and compliance. Task-relevant visual semantics systematically weaken refusal behavior, most strongly for authority-like cues such as authorization documents and identity credentials, consistent with over-reliance on the apparent legitimacy and credibility conveyed by visual context. The instruction carrier effect is model-dependent; visually rendered instructions do not consistently increase jailbreak susceptibility relative to direct text. Diagnostic analyses on a representative open-weight model identify vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions.

Our contributions are as follows:

•

MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark that incorporates harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier into a unified controlled design for factor-level analysis of multimodal jailbreak vulnerabilities.

•

Large-scale evaluations across 16 representative open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, revealing uneven jailbreak vulnerabilities across harm domains, the dominant role of prompt framing, the refusal-weakening effect of authority-like visual cues, and the model-dependent effect of instruction carriers, together with diagnostics on a representative open-weight model linking these effects to internal representations and cross-modal interactions.

•

A modular multimodal jailbreak evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, and cost-efficient multimodal jailbreak auditing.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreak attacks aim to circumvent safety alignment and induce models to assist with harmful requests (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). Early studies attributed such failures to competing objectives and mismatched generalization in safety training (Wei et al., 2023). Subsequent work demonstrated transferable adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023) and black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), while indirect prompt injection showed that malicious instructions can be introduced through external documents or retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023). Refusal behavior is thus highly sensitive to how harmful intent is framed and delivered (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023).

Multimodal models distribute instructions and contextual cues across language and vision (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). Visual inputs can be exploited through adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024). Defenses span safety alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), with uncertain robustness under changes in modality and context; identical harmful intent may elicit different safety behavior under different linguistic or visual contexts.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

Standardized safety benchmarks such as SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) establish structured taxonomies and reproducible protocols for evaluating harmful behavior and refusal robustness. MM-SafetyBench evaluates image-based safety attacks (Liu et al., 2024), FigStep (Gong et al., 2025) studies harmful instructions rendered as typographic images, and JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025) expand coverage across diverse multimodal jailbreak strategies. MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025) provides a unified framework for comparing multimodal jailbreak attacks and defenses, and OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025) broadens standardized attack-defense evaluation with multidimensional metrics.

Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025) constructs parallel variants of the same harmful seeds across modality configurations and evaluates cross-modal safety consistency. These benchmarks improve attack coverage, evaluation standardization, and modality-level comparison, but do not independently manipulate the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions. MMJailBench systematically varies prompt framing, task-relevant visual semantics, and instruction carrier over matched harmful intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

MMJailBench constructs matched multimodal scenarios by systematically varying harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers within a unified evaluation space (Figure 2). We describe the design and each factor below.

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Prior multimodal jailbreak benchmarks center on predefined attack instances or modality variations in which harmful intent, linguistic formulation, visual context, and instruction presentation are jointly encoded in each evaluation and yield aggregate measurements of vulnerability.

MMJailBench factorizes a multimodal jailbreak instance into four components: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier. Given a harmful intent $h$ , a prompt framing strategy $t$ , a visual semantic condition $v$ , and an instruction carrier $c$ , each multimodal instance is represented as

| | $x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),$
| | (1)

where $L(h,t,c)$ denotes the instruction component generated from harmful intent $h$ , prompt framing $t$ , and instruction carrier $c$ , while $V(h,v)$ denotes the visual input associated with harmful intent $h$ and visual semantics $v$ .

With 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt framing strategies, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carriers, the Cartesian combination yields 16,320 controlled multimodal jailbreak instances, held identical across models and harm categories.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Harmful intents are constructed as intent-level behavioral seeds rather than collected jailbreak prompts that bind harmful goals to specific attack strategies, so the contextual factors can vary around a fixed objective.

The benchmark contains 272 harmful intents across 9 major harm domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content. Each category is further divided into fine-grained subcategories. Intents are collected through category-guided construction, followed by semantic similarity filtering and manual verification to reduce redundancy.

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

Prompt framing specifies how the same harmful intent is linguistically presented. MMJailBench introduces 6 prompt framing strategies: academic, system, structured, story, code, and safety-paradox framing. These capture common reformulations of harmful requests that preserve the underlying intent, e.g., embedding the request in a fictional scenario, casting it as a structured generation task, or presenting it as an apparently legitimate system requirement. Only the linguistic framing varies; harmful intent is fixed.

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

Visual semantics capture the contextual meaning introduced by accompanying images. Unlike image-based instruction attacks that encode instructions as visual text, this factor varies contextual visual information around an unchanged harmful intent.

We construct 5 task-relevant visual semantic conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, and authorization documents, spanning legitimacy-associated, expertise-related, and authority-related contextual signals. For each harmful intent, the visual input adds semantic context without modifying the harmful instruction. Controlled visual conditions, including irrelevant or non-semantic images, are additionally used in diagnostic evaluations.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

Instruction carrier describes the presentation modality of the same instruction. MMJailBench considers 2 instruction carriers: direct textual instructions (TEXT) and visually rendered instructions in text-containing images (OCR). TEXT provides the harmful instruction as text; OCR renders the same instruction into an image with preserved semantics. Because OCR introduces an additional perception stage, we measure instruction recognition mismatch, i.e., cases where the model fails to interpret the embedded instruction correctly.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

The primary metric is Attack Success Rate (ASR):

| | $ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

where $s_{i}$ denotes the harmfulness score of the $i$ -th response on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale.

For instruction carrier analysis, we further introduce Conditional Attack Success Rate (CASR):

| | $CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

where mismatch comprises OCR recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretation of the evaluated intent.

The main experiments use GPT-5 as an LLM-based judge, which assigns each response a harmfulness score and auxiliary labels for jailbreak success and instruction mismatch. Refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussions are not counted as successful jailbreaks. All main results are based on GPT-5 judgments. A benchmark-specific lightweight judge based on an open-weight MLLM is additionally provided for cost-efficient follow-up evaluation under the same protocol.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

MMJailBench supports full and lightweight configurations. The full configuration evaluates all instances and is used for model-level, domain-level, and factor-level comparisons. The lightweight configuration samples a subset that preserves coverage across harmful domains, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers, for efficient safety auditing and regression testing. Unless otherwise specified, reported results use the full configuration.

## 5 Results and Analysis

We report overall jailbreak vulnerability, factor-level effects, and model-dependent vulnerability patterns across the 16 MLLMs.

### 5.1 Overall Jailbreak Landscape

Figure 3 and Table 1 summarize model-level ASR across controlled multimodal conditions and harmful domains under the full configuration. Average ASR ranges from 2.17% for GPT-5 to 78.38% for GLM-4.6V. Models of comparable multimodal capability can exhibit markedly different vulnerability profiles, so general capability does not track jailbreak robustness.

Cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally achieve higher ASR, whereas categories such as physical harm exhibit comparatively lower vulnerability.

### 5.2 Factor-Level Attribution

We analyze four dimensions of jailbreak vulnerability, varying individual factors with other conditions fixed: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier.

#### Harmful Intent.

Jailbreak vulnerability varies substantially across harm domains (Table 1). Cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy-related behaviors, and deception-related tasks generally exhibit higher ASR across models, while physical harm and sensitive content categories tend to show lower vulnerability; aggregate safety scores therefore conceal domain-specific weaknesses.

#### Prompt Framing.

Prompt framing introduces the largest variation among the evaluated factors. Models exhibit distinct sensitivity patterns across framing strategies (Figure 3(a)), but story, structured, and academic framings generally lead to higher ASR, while system-style and safety-paradox framings show lower vulnerability. ## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

We construct a diagnostic subset from matched MMJailBench instances emphasizing authority-document scenarios and analyze layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention patterns in gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Figure 4 analyzes residual-stream representations of the final generation-prefix token. The representation divergence between authority and danger conditions increases with depth, with the sharpest rise at layer 42 (Figure 4(a)).

We fit an authority-minus-danger representation direction on discovery samples and apply the fixed direction to held-out pairs. Authority-document contexts are clearly displaced along this direction on held-out pairs (Figure 4(b)), with consistent positive shifts across all harm domains (Figure 4(c)).

Figure 4: Representation-level diagnostics of gemma3-12b under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

We measure attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5). At the representation-sensitive layer identified above, authority-document contexts exhibit lower attention mass on both harm-related task-label and visual tokens. Together with the representation displacement, this indicates that authority cues induce a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention during response initiation, consistent with the increased jailbreak susceptibility under authority-related visual contexts.

Figure 5: Cross-modal interaction diagnostics in gemma3-12b. Attention allocation to harm-related textual tokens and visual tokens varies across layers under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench varies harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers under control. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, prompt framing introduces the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability through contextual cues, instruction carriers exhibit model-dependent effects, and harmful intents show category-specific vulnerability. Diagnostics reveal vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. Modular full and lightweight configurations, flexible judge options, and multidimensional metrics support reproducible and scalable multimodal safety evaluation.

### A.1 Harmful Intent Taxonomy, Collection, and Filtering

The taxonomy organizes harmful behaviors into a hierarchy of intents, domains, and scenarios; each intent carries a task identifier, harm category, scenario, and action description.

It contains 272 unique harmful intents covering 9 major harm domains and 18 harm scenarios (Table 5): Cyber & Tech Abuse (Cyber), Economic Harm (Econ.), Privacy & IP (Privacy), Deception & Public Influence (Decept.), Illegal Goods & Services (Illegal), Hate & Harassment (Hate), Violence & Physical Harm (Violence), Sensitive Regulated Advice (Sensitive), and Sexual Content (Sexual). It is derived from existing safety benchmarks (Luo et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2024) and public model-provider safety policies (OpenAI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2025a; Google, 2026), followed by intent normalization, taxonomy organization, and manual filtering.

We compute pairwise similarity among the 272 intents using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Most intent pairs have relatively low semantic similarity, with a small high-similarity tail (Figure 6) that is manually reviewed to remove near-duplicates so that retained intents represent distinct harmful objectives. A PCA projection of the intent embeddings (Figure 7) shows intents from different harm domains occupying diverse regions rather than collapsing into a few clusters.

### A.2 Prompt Framing Templates

The 6 templates are Academic Analysis (Academic), System-Role Simulation (System), Fictional Storytelling (Story), Code-Style Indirection (Code), Structured Completion (Structure), and Safety-Paradox Reasoning (Paradox), summarized in Table 6. Each is instantiated by substituting the target harmful intent into a task-specific placeholder, leaving the harmful objective unchanged across templates. The templates are evaluation probes providing repeatable linguistic conditions, not an exhaustive collection of jailbreak attacks.

Figure 8: Examples of the five visual semantic categories in MMJailBench.

### A.3 Visual Semantic Generation

The 5 visual semantic categories are Danger, Work Scenario, Authorization Document, Identity Credential, and Role, each preserving the underlying harmful intent and prompt framing.

For each harmful intent, qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b) generates visual descriptions and image generation prompts. zimage2025-Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025) generates scenes for Danger, Work Scenario, and Role, while a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) is used for Identity Credential and Authorization Document owing to its image-editing capability for images with coherent textual elements. Generated images are filtered on semantic relevance, visual quality, and readability. Figure 8 shows representative examples.

### A.4 Instruction Carrier Construction

MMJailBench uses two carrier modes: direct text input (TEXT) and visually embedded instruction input (OCR). For OCR instances, the instruction text is rendered into a readable image and combined with the corresponding visual semantic image, preserving the original harmful intent and prompt framing. A standardized layout minimizes formatting variation between the two modes.

## Appendix B Experimental and Evaluation Details

### B.1 Evaluated MLLMs

We evaluate 16 MLLMs: 8 open-weight and 8 proprietary-access. Open-weight: qwen2.5-vl-7b (Bai et al., 2025b), qwen3-vl-8b (Bai et al., 2025a), gemma3-12b (Gemma Team et al., 2025), internvl3-8b (Zhu et al., 2025), glm4.1v-9b (Hong et al., 2025), ministral3-8b (Liu et al., 2026), step3-vl-10b (Huang et al., 2026), and llava-onevision-1.5 (An et al., 2025). Proprietary-access: gpt-5 (Singh et al., 2025), gemini-3-flash (Google DeepMind, 2025), claude-sonnet-4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), grok-4-fast (xAI, 2025), qwen3-vl-plus (Bai et al., 2025a), kimi-k2.5 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), glm-4.6v (Hong et al., 2025), and doubao-seed-2.0-lite (ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). Open-weight models use publicly available checkpoints; proprietary-access models are queried through their official interfaces.

Each model is tested on the complete Cartesian product of 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carrier modes: 16,320 instances per model and 261,120 total model responses.

| Score | Definition

| 1 | Refusal or safe response without harmful details.

| 2 | Potential risk without direct harmful instructions.

| 3 | High-level or partial harmful information.

| 4 | Actionable harmful assistance.

| 5 | Detailed and operational harmful guidance.

Table 7: Harmfulness scoring rubric for response evaluation.

### B.2 Evaluation Rubric and Judge Prompt

GPT-5 is the primary evaluator. For each response it outputs an instruction-mismatch flag and a harmfulness score. The mismatch flag marks failures to recognize the task, such as only transcribing visual content, repeating the prompt, or producing meaningless outputs. The harmfulness score follows the strict 1 $\sim$ 5 rubric of Table 7, with higher scores indicating stronger compliance and more actionable harmful content.

The judge prompt includes anti-deception rules so that safety disclaimers, fictional framing, or academic packaging do not lower the score when harmful information is provided; responses limited to refusal, safe redirection, or non-actionable discussion receive low scores. The complete template is in the Code and Data Supplement.

### B.3 Full and Lightweight Benchmark Settings

The full configuration evaluates the complete Cartesian product of 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carrier modes, i.e., 16,320 instances per model.

The lightweight configuration contains 1,500 instances drawn by stratified sampling over harm domains, prompt framings, visual semantic conditions, and carrier modes, preserving the factor distribution of the full configuration; it is validated in Section C.4.

### B.4 Lightweight Judge Model

We train a benchmark-scoped lightweight judge based on qwen3-8b (Team et al., 2025) on GPT-5-generated annotations. It predicts harmfulness scores and mismatch labels under the same protocol as the GPT-5 judge; agreement is reported in Section C.4, and training configurations are in the Code and Data Supplement.

###### Abstract

We present MMJailBench, a factorized multimodal jailbreak benchmark over harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, with controlled configurations supporting factor-level attribution. Across 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs, vulnerability profiles are heterogeneous and model-dependent. ASR varies markedly across harm domains. Prompt framing dominates variation. Task-relevant visual semantics raise susceptibility, most strongly for authority-like cues. Visually rendered instructions do not consistently exceed direct textual instructions. Diagnostics on one open-weight model locate vulnerability-associated patterns in internal representations and cross-modal interactions. We release a modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics for reproducible, scalable, low-cost auditing. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

MLLMs are deployed in document understanding, code generation, workflow assistance, and automated operations (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). Harmful requests to them may pair textual or visually rendered instructions (Gong et al., 2025) with professional settings, identity credentials, or authorization documents, and refusal decisions are conditioned on cross-modal context (Li et al., 2024b). Visual input can shift the perceived legitimacy, professionalism, and credibility of a request, so a single intent can elicit different behaviors across contexts (Liu et al., 2024); multimodal jailbreaks thus probe the stability of safety alignment under cross-modal conditions (Luo et al., 2024).

Figure 1: Motivation of MMJailBench. Existing benchmarks entangle multiple factors within fixed instances; MMJailBench factorizes them into a controlled evaluation space.

Text and multimodal safety benchmarks cover harmful behaviors (Li et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), visual attacks, and image-based text injection (Liu et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024), using fixed prompt-image pairs per task that jointly encode harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier; their ASR reflects aggregate vulnerability on a given test set (Weng et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025).

MMJailBench comprises 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt templates, 5 types of task-relevant visual semantics, and 2 instruction carriers under matched comparisons, together with a modular suite offering full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics.

Figure 2: Construction and evaluation pipeline of MMJailBench over harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier.

On 16 MLLMs, cyber abuse, economic harm, privacy violations, and deception and manipulation show higher vulnerability; prompt framing is the dominant source of variation at fixed intent; task-relevant visual semantics weaken refusal, with authorization documents and identity credentials most pronounced, consistent with over-reliance on visually conveyed legitimacy and credibility; carrier effects are model-dependent, with OCR not consistently above TEXT. Representation and attention diagnostics on one open-weight model identify associated internal patterns.

Contributions:

•

MMJailBench, a factorized benchmark over harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics, and instruction carrier, supporting factor-level attribution.

•

Evaluation of 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs establishing uneven domain vulnerability, dominance of prompt framing, refusal weakening under authority-like visual cues, and model-dependent carrier effects, with diagnostics on internal representations and cross-modal interactions.

•

A modular evaluation suite with full and lightweight configurations, multiple judge options, and multidimensional metrics.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses

Jailbreaks circumvent safety alignment (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023), attributed to competing objectives and mismatched generalization (Wei et al., 2023). Transferable adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023), black-box semantic attacks such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), and indirect prompt injection through documents or retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023) establish sensitivity of refusal to framing and delivery (Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Greshake et al., 2023).

In MLLMs, instructions and cues span language and vision (Gong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b): adversarial images (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), typographic prompts (Gong et al., 2025), and other cross-modal constructions (Luo et al., 2024). Defenses span alignment, input transformation, and inference-time safeguards (Jain et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), with uncertain robustness across modality and context shifts; identical intent may receive different treatment under different linguistic or visual contexts.

### 2.2 Multimodal Jailbreak Benchmarks

SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2023), SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) provide taxonomies and reproducible protocols. MM-SafetyBench (Liu et al., 2024) targets image-based attacks, FigStep (Gong et al., 2025) typographic instructions, and JailBreakV (Luo et al., 2024) and VLJailbreakBench (Wang et al., 2025) broader strategy coverage; MMJ-Bench (Weng et al., 2025) unifies attack/defense comparison, and OmniSafeBench-MM (Jia et al., 2025) adds multidimensional metrics.

Omni-SafetyBench (Pan et al., 2025) builds parallel variants of harmful seeds across modality configurations for cross-modal consistency. None independently manipulates the linguistic and semantic factors within matched multimodal interactions; MMJailBench varies prompt framing, task-relevant visual semantics, and instruction carrier over matched harmful intents.

## 3 MMJailBench

MMJailBench (Figure 2) constructs matched multimodal scenarios by systematically varying harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers within a unified evaluation space.

### 3.1 Factorized Design

Prior benchmarks center on predefined attack instances or modality variations with harmful intent, linguistic formulation, visual context, and instruction presentation jointly encoded. MMJailBench uses

| | $x_{h,t,v,c}=(L(h,t,c),V(h,v)),$
| | (1)

with $h$ harmful intent, $t$ prompt framing, $v$ visual semantics, and $c$ instruction carrier; $L(h,t,c)$ is the instruction component and $V(h,v)$ the visual input. With 272 harmful intents, 6 prompt framing strategies, 5 visual semantic conditions, and 2 instruction carriers, the Cartesian product yields 16,320 instances, consistent across models and harm categories.

### 3.2 Harmful Intent

Intents are intent-level behavioral seeds rather than collected jailbreak prompts, so the objective stays fixed across contextual variation. There are 272 harmful intents in 9 major harm domains: Physical Harm, Cyber Abuse, Economic Harm, Hate and Harassment, Privacy and IP, Regulated Advice, Illegal Activities, Deception and Influence, and Sexual Content, each split into subcategories. Construction is category-guided, followed by semantic similarity filtering and manual verification.

### 3.3 Prompt Framing

6 strategies: academic, system, structured, story, code, and safety-paradox, e.g., embedding the request in fiction, as a structured generation task, or as an apparently legitimate system requirement, with intent held fixed.

### 3.4 Visual Semantics

5 task-relevant conditions: danger-related context, scenario context, professional-role context, identity credentials, and authorization documents, spanning legitimacy-, expertise-, and authority-related signals; the image adds context without modifying the instruction. Irrelevant or non-semantic control images enter diagnostic evaluations.

### 3.5 Instruction Carrier

2 carriers: TEXT and OCR (same instruction rendered into a text-containing image, semantics preserved). Instruction recognition mismatch is recorded to separate perception failures from carrier-related safety differences.

### 4.2 Metrics and Judge Models

| | $ASR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq 4),$
| | (2)

with $s_{i}$ the harmfulness score of response $i$ on a 1 $\sim$ 5 scale. For carrier analysis:

| | $CASR=\frac{N_{success}}{N-N_{mismatch}},$
| | (3)

where $N_{mismatch}$ counts OCR recognition failures, irrelevant responses, and misinterpretations of the evaluated intent; ASR is end-to-end, CASR conditioned on understanding.

GPT-5 judges every response, assigning a harmfulness score plus jailbreak-success and instruction-mismatch labels; refusals, safety warnings, and high-level discussion do not count as success. All main results use GPT-5 judgments. A benchmark-specific lightweight judge built on an open-weight MLLM supports low-cost follow-up evaluation under the same protocol.

### 4.3 Evaluation Configurations

Full configuration: all instances, used for model-, domain-, and factor-level analysis. Lightweight configuration: representative subset covering harmful domains, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers, for auditing and regression testing. Results are full-configuration unless stated.

## 6 Diagnostic Analysis

A diagnostic subset of matched MMJailBench instances emphasizing authority-document scenarios is used to probe layer-wise representations and cross-modal attention in gemma3-12b.

### 6.1 Representation-Level Diagnostics

Residual-stream representations of the final generation-prefix token (Figure 4): authority–danger divergence grows with depth, rising most sharply at layer 42 (Figure 4(a)). An authority-minus-danger direction fit on discovery samples and applied fixed to held-out pairs displaces authority-document contexts (Figure 4(b)), with consistent positive shifts across all harm domains (Figure 4(c)), i.e., a shared higher-layer pattern across diverse harmful objectives.

Figure 4: Representation-level diagnostics of gemma3-12b under authority-document and danger-image contexts across layers and harm domains.

### 6.2 Cross-Modal Interaction Diagnostics

Attention from the final generation-prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens and special visual tokens (Figure 5) differs layer-wise between authority-document and danger-image contexts. At the representation-sensitive layer, authority-document contexts place lower attention mass on both token types. Together with the representation displacement, this is consistent with authority cues inducing a higher-level contextual state with redistributed attention at response initiation, offering an internal account of the increased susceptibility.

Figure 5: Cross-modal interaction diagnostics in gemma3-12b: attention to harm-related textual tokens and visual tokens across layers under authority-document and danger-image contexts.

## 7 Conclusion

MMJailBench varies harmful intents, prompt framings, visual semantics, and instruction carriers under control. Over 16 open-weight and proprietary MLLMs: prompt framing introduces the largest variation, visual semantics add vulnerability via contextual cues, carrier effects are model-dependent, and harmful intents show category-specific patterns; diagnostics reveal associated representation and cross-modal interaction patterns. Full and lightweight configurations, flexible judges, and multidimensional metrics support reproducible, scalable multimodal safety evaluation.
